When the mind wanders in harmony with Heaven, this is what is called overcoming through reverence and not letting indolence prevail; when principle and the person revolve together in close accord, not only does one not dare to be idle, one also has no leisure to be idle. Such was Zhongzong's…

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
善凝天命而對越之也君德所以懋而享年所
由永與嗣王監之哉抑人主守成志易盈於豐
泰一有不敬侈肆乘之則保泰持盈誠莫敬爲
要也中宗以繼體之君而知此得日躋之家法
矣成王非守成者耶以中宗爲可法也則敬止
執競之遺矩昭昭也噫疑亦當時敷訓意也
詩
之綱之紀燕及朋友百辟卿士媚于天子
不解于位民之攸塈　荊州俊
===
同考試官教諭李　批〔題意重明良保泰此作攄發透朗而詞氣爾雅詩人忠愛之意溢於言表取之不獨以其文也〕
考試官教諭王　批〔詞意剴切脉絡融貫〕
考試官教諭趙　批〔精鍊古雅〕
王者克盡君道而臣民胥賴焉夫君道莫大於
綱紀也綱紀振於上而臣民舉安矣此盛世之
事而詩人爲嗣王願也意曰王者首出庶物而
統理臣民非以其位之足以震天下以其道之
punctuated:
善凝天命而對越之也。君德所以懋，而享年所由永與！嗣王監之哉！抑人主守成，志易盈於豐泰。一有不敬，侈肆乘之，則保泰持盈，誠莫敬爲要也。中宗以繼體之君而知此，得日躋之家法矣。成王非守成者耶？以中宗爲可法也，則敬止執競之遺矩昭昭也。噫！疑亦當時敷訓意也。

詩
「之綱之紀，燕及朋友。百辟卿士，媚于天子。不解于位，民之攸塈。」　荊州俊
同考試官教諭李　批〔題意重明良保泰，此作攄發透朗，而詞氣爾雅，詩人忠愛之意溢於言表，取之不獨以其文也。〕
考試官教諭王　批〔詞意剴切，脉絡融貫。〕
考試官教諭趙　批〔精鍊古雅。〕

王者克盡君道，而臣民胥賴焉。夫君道莫大於綱紀也，綱紀振於上，而臣民舉安矣。此盛世之事，而詩人爲嗣王願也。意曰：王者首出庶物而統理臣民，非以其位之足以震天下，以其道之
translation_en:
…ably consolidating the Mandate of Heaven and standing in reverent response to it. Is this not whereby the ruler's virtue was made great and the years of his reign prolonged! Let the succeeding king take this as his mirror! Moreover, when a sovereign preserves an established heritage, his mind easily grows self-satisfied amidst abundance and peace. Once there is a lapse in reverence, extravagance and license take advantage of it; thus for preserving peace and maintaining fullness, truly nothing is more essential than reverence. That Zhongzong, as a ruler inheriting the throne, understood this shows he had grasped the family tradition of daily ascending in virtue. Was King Cheng not also a preserver of an established heritage? If he took Zhongzong as a model to follow, then the bequeathed standards of resting in reverence and holding fast to vigorous effort were bright and clear. Alas! I suspect this too was the intention behind the instruction set forth at the time.

Classic of Poetry (Shijing)
"He gives law and order to the kingdom, bringing repose even to his friends. All the feudal princes and ministers show their devoted love to the Son of Heaven; not slackening in their offices, they give the people rest." — Jing Zhoujun 荊州俊

Associate Examiner and Instructor Li 李 comments: [The import of the topic emphasizes an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers preserving great peace. This composition develops the theme with penetrating clarity, and its diction and spirit are refined and classical. The poet's loyal and affectionate intent overflows beyond the words; it is selected not merely for its literary style.]
Examiner and Instructor Wang 王 comments: [The wording and meaning are incisive and pertinent; the thread of thought is thoroughly coherent.]
Examiner and Instructor Zhao 趙 comments: [Refined, succinct, and classically elegant.]

When a true king is able to fulfill the Way of the ruler to the utmost, both subjects and people alike rely upon him. Now, nothing in the Way of the ruler is greater than the overarching laws and regulations (gangji); when the laws and regulations are invigorated from above, subjects and people are all brought to peace. This is the affair of a flourishing age, and what the poet wished for the succeeding king. The meaning is as follows: When a true king rises preeminent above the multitude of things to govern subjects and people, it is not because his position is sufficient to overawe the world, but because his Way…

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
足以安天下耳茲惟嗣王脩德任賢而爲四方
之綱焉將見乾綱運於一人則道揆立而又安
之化以溥國紀昭於五位則法守一而輯寧之
治以弘維皇建天下之極而羣工承其休贊襄
於朝廷之上惟見其欽若焉耳矣大君執天下
之樞而百寮宣其化承宣於邦國之間惟見其
仰成焉耳矣何燕如之由是百辟卿士荷覆冒
之仁而愛戴之心彌篤切圖報之義而忠藎之
志愈殷以爲綱之張也一或解焉則弛尤必厲
===
憂勤於無斁而一日履其位則一日立其綱俾
民之待命於我者永有所庇焉可也紀之理也
一或解焉則紊尤必持兢業於勿替而一日居
其位則一日陳其紀俾民之望治於我者永有
所依焉可也蓋必如是而後吾人媚茲之忱始
慰吾君燕及之仁亦未艾矣寧非我周極盛之
治哉嗟乎此人君御世之大權也民之休戚世
之治亂恒必由之人臣以是媚其君非所謂忠
而知誨者耶厥後王政不綱小國困弊而天下
punctuated: 足以安天下耳。茲惟嗣王脩德任賢，而爲四方之綱焉。將見乾綱運於一人，則道揆立而又安之化以溥；國紀昭於五位，則法守一而輯寧之治以弘。維皇建天下之極，而羣工承其休，贊襄於朝廷之上，惟見其欽若焉耳矣；大君執天下之樞，而百寮宣其化，承宣於邦國之間，惟見其仰成焉耳矣。何燕如之！由是百辟卿士，荷覆冒之仁而愛戴之心彌篤，切圖報之義而忠藎之志愈殷。以爲綱之張也，一或解焉則弛，尤必厲憂勤於無斁，而一日履其位，則一日立其綱，俾民之待命於我者，永有所庇焉可也；紀之理也，一或解焉則紊，尤必持兢業於勿替，而一日居其位，則一日陳其紀，俾民之望治於我者，永有所依焉可也。蓋必如是，而後吾人媚茲之忱始慰，吾君燕及之仁亦未艾矣。寧非我周極盛之治哉！嗟乎！此人君御世之大權也，民之休戚、世之治亂，恒必由之。人臣以是媚其君，非所謂忠而知誨者耶？厥後王政不綱，小國困弊，而天下
translation_en:
…is sufficient to bring peace to All under Heaven. Now, as the succeeding king cultivates virtue and employs the worthy, acting as the guiding rope and mesh for the four quarters, one will see the sovereign head-rope wielded by the One Man, whereby the measure of the Way is established and the transforming influence of peace and security [reading 乂安 for 又安] is widely diffused; and the state regulations made manifest from the Fifth Position [the throne], whereby adherence to the laws is unified and the governance of harmony and tranquility is broadened. The august sovereign establishes the supreme standard of the world, and the multitude of officials receive his blessings—assisting at court above, they are seen only to reverently accord with him! The great ruler holds the pivot of the world, and the hundred officers proclaim his transforming influence—receiving and proclaiming it among the states and domains, they are seen only to look up to his accomplishments! What repose could compare to this!

From this, the hundred lords and noble officers, bearing his all-covering benevolence, grow ever firmer in their hearts of love and devotion; keenly feeling their duty to repay him, they become ever more earnest in their aspirations of loyal service. They consider that in the stretching of the head-rope, if there is a single moment of slackening it will go limp; therefore he must all the more rouse himself to anxious diligence without wearying: for every day he occupies his position, for that day he must establish its head-rope, so that the people who await their fate from us may forever have shelter—only thus will it do. And in the ordering of the mesh-cords, if there is a single moment of slackening they will fall into tangle; therefore he must all the more maintain cautious reverence without fail: for every day he dwells in his position, for that day he must set forth its mesh-cords, so that the people who hope for good governance from us may forever have something to rely upon—only thus will it do. Indeed, only when it is like this will our sincere affection for him finally be comforted, and our lord's benevolence in extending repose to others be unending. Would this not be the most flourishing governance of our Zhou dynasty!

Alas! This is the great prerogative by which a ruler governs the world; the weal and woe of the people, the order and disorder of the age, invariably depend upon it. When a minister shows affection for his ruler by such means, is he not what is called loyal and knowing how to instruct? Thereafter, royal governance lost its guiding rope, the smaller states fell into distress and exhaustion, and in the world…

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
多失所之民焉至於黍離下泉之咏興而後知
綱紀不解之說爲慮遠矣
日就月將學有緝熙于光明佛時仔肩示
我顯德行
李都生
同考試官教諭李　批　發成王勉敬求助意爽朗透徹而詞復雅練是深於詩者
考試官教諭王　批　典雅莊嚴
考試官教諭趙　批　意明體整
===
賢王之勉敬也旣勵其功於巳復求其助於人
蓋敬者人君所以存天之道也合人巳而交脩勉敬
之功至矣此成王所以保天命也想其答羣臣
之戒有曰敬之爲道大矣聚之則爲光明之體
運之則爲顯明之德人君之所賴以勝其任者
恒於斯也維予小子不以質之不聰自委也而
顯道之祇承思翼翼以鼓其進不以敬之未能
自安也而明命之顧諟期亹亹以繼其功學之
於月欲有所就焉尤必與日俱積務俾一眞之
punctuated:
多失所之民焉。至於《黍離》、《下泉》之咏興，而後知綱紀不解之說爲慮遠矣。

「日就月將，學有緝熙于光明。佛時仔肩，示我顯德行。」
李都生
同考試官教諭李　批：發成王勉敬求助意，爽朗透徹，而詞復雅練，是深於《詩》者。
考試官教諭王　批：典雅莊嚴。
考試官教諭趙　批：意明體整。

賢王之勉敬也，旣勵其功於巳，復求其助於人。蓋敬者，人君所以存天之道也。合人巳而交脩，勉敬之功至矣，此成王所以保天命也。想其答羣臣之戒，有曰：敬之爲道大矣！聚之則爲光明之體，運之則爲顯明之德，人君之所賴以勝其任者，恒於斯也。維予小子，不以質之不聰自委也，而顯道之祇承，思翼翼以鼓其進；不以敬之未能自安也，而明命之顧諟，期亹亹以繼其功。學之於月，欲有所就焉，尤必與日俱積，務俾一眞之
translation_en:
… there were many displaced people. Only when the songs of "Millet" (Shuli) and "Flowing Spring" (Xiaquan) arose did one realize how far-sighted was the doctrine of never relaxing the guiding ropes and governing threads.

"With daily accomplishment and monthly progress, may my learning have continuous brightness unto illumination. Help me bear this burden upon my shoulders, and show me how to display virtuous conduct."
Li Dusheng 
Associate Examiner, Instructor Li, comments: He brings out King Cheng's intention of striving for reverence and seeking assistance in a clear, penetrating manner, while his phrasing is also refined and polished; he is one deeply versed in the Odes.
Examiner, Instructor Wang, comments: Classically elegant and solemn.
Examiner, Instructor Zhao, comments: The meaning is clear and the structure is well-ordered.

When the worthy king strove for reverence, he not only exerted his own effort in himself, but also sought assistance from others. For reverence is the Way by which a ruler preserves Heaven. By combining others and oneself in mutual cultivation, the effort of striving for reverence reaches its utmost; this was how King Cheng preserved the Mandate of Heaven. One may imagine him replying to the admonitions of his assembled ministers, saying: Great indeed is the Way of reverence! Gathered within, it forms a luminous substance; put into operation, it becomes manifest virtue. That upon which a ruler relies to be equal to his burden always lies herein. I, the little child, do not excuse myself on account of my unintelligent nature; rather, in reverently receiving the manifest Way, I think cautiously and carefully of spurring my progress. Nor do I rest content in my inability to attain reverence; rather, in keeping my eyes upon the bright Mandate, I hope tirelessly to continue the work. In my learning by the day [?; text reads 月, "month"], wishing to achieve something therein, I must all the more accumulate it with each passing day, striving to make the crystalline clarity of the one truth …

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
瑩徹與顯思而相昭格斯已矣學之於月欲有
所將焉尤必與月俱進務俾萬境之昭融與日
監而相對越斯已矣夫勉敬者固小子志矣而
輔德者非諸臣責耶當念予繼序之惟艱而時
勤啓沃閔予基命之不易而各効贊襄顯道之
具於人此德行之不容昧者爾其詔之以開予
之蒙焉則就將之功有所從入而聰明其漸啓
乎明命之體於人此德行之不容晦者爾其示
之以覺予之迷焉則緝熙之學有所持循而光
===
明其漸進乎夫然則仔肩之重可勝不易之命
可保諸臣之所告戒與予之所訪落斯爲無負
矣吁此成王所以爲守成之令主也歟雖然有
自來矣文之敬止武之執競此周之家法也成
王能紹二后之心傳以撫二后之基業周家有
道之長豈偶然哉至於臣戒其君惟恐其不能
君望於臣惟恐其不盡又宛然虞庭交儆之風
焉盛世君臣之相與固如此使後王能世守之
周雖至今存可也
punctuated: 瑩徹，與顯思而相昭格斯已矣；學之於月欲有所將焉，尤必與月俱進，務俾萬境之昭融，與日監而相對越斯已矣。夫勉敬者，固小子志矣；而輔德者，非諸臣責耶？當念予繼序之惟艱，而時勤啓沃；閔予基命之不易，而各効贊襄。顯道之具於人，此德行之不容昧者，爾其詔之以開予之蒙焉，則就將之功有所從入，而聰明其漸啓乎！明命之體於人，此德行之不容晦者，爾其示之以覺予之迷焉，則緝熙之學有所持循，而光明其漸進乎！夫然，則仔肩之重可勝，不易之命可保，諸臣之所告戒，與予之所訪落，斯爲無負矣。」吁！此成王所以爲守成之令主也歟！雖然，有自來矣。文之敬止，武之執競，此周之家法也。成王能紹二后之心傳，以撫二后之基業，周家有道之長，豈偶然哉！至於臣戒其君，惟恐其不能；君望於臣，惟恐其不盡，又宛然虞庭交儆之風焉。盛世君臣之相與，固如此。使後王能世守之，周雖至今存可也。
translation_en:
…crystalline clarity mutually illuminates and communes with what is gloriously manifest, and only then will I rest; in studying by the month and wishing to advance in it [Note: the transcription reads 月 (month) where the parallel phrase on the previous page also read 月 for 日 (day)], I must all the more progress with each passing month, striving to make the bright harmony of all realms respond in reverence to Heaven's daily inspection, and only then will I rest. Now, to strive for reverence is indeed the aspiration of me, the little child; yet is not assisting my virtue the responsibility of all you ministers? You should bear in mind the difficulty of my continuing the royal line, and constantly be diligent in enlightening and nourishing me; you should commiserate with how hard it is for me to establish the Mandate, and each offer your assistance and support. The manifest Way as it is complete in man—this is virtuous conduct that must not be obscured; may you instruct me in it so as to open up my ignorance! Then my effort of daily achievement and monthly advance will have an entry point, and will not my intelligence gradually be opened? The bright Mandate as it is embodied in man—this is virtuous conduct that must not be darkened; may you show me it so as to awaken me from my confusion! Then my learning of continuous illumination will have something to hold fast to and follow, and will not my radiant light gradually advance? If it is thus, then the heavy burden on my shoulders can be borne, the unchanging Mandate can be preserved, and neither the admonitions of you ministers nor my own inaugural consultations will have been in vain."

Ah! Is this not how King Cheng (Chengwang 成王) became an exemplary ruler in preserving what had been achieved? Even so, it had its origin. King Wen's (Wenwang 文王) resting in reverence and King Wu's (Wuwang 武王) holding fast with vigor—these were the family traditions of the Zhou. Since King Cheng was able to continue the transmission of the mind-and-heart of those two sovereigns so as to soothe and govern the foundational enterprise of the two sovereigns, how could the enduring length of the Zhou house's virtuous rule have been accidental? As for the ministers admonishing their ruler, fearing only that he might prove incapable, and the ruler looking to his ministers, fearing only that they might not give their utmost—this too was the very image of the mutual admonition at the court of Yu [Shun 舜]. Such indeed was the fellowship between ruler and ministers in a flourishing age. Had later kings been able to guard it generation after generation, the Zhou might well have survived even down to the present day!

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
春秋
夏齊侯衛侯胥命于蒲〔桓公三年〕楚屈完
來盟于師盟于召陵〔僖公四年〕
成以蒙
同考試官教諭謝　批〔詞雅詞峻且發聖人不貴盟戰〕
考試官教諭王　批〔嚴整瑩潔〕
考試官教諭趙　批〔詞調雄渾〕
〔意委曲詳盡可以式矣〕
以信相諭者春秋善之以禮服遠者春秋美之
===
此蒲之信召陵之禮均爲近於古也且于蒲何
命齊衛以牧伯相推也春秋善之者何蓋信以
發志信不足而從事于盟風之所以日漓也矧
齊衛當兩伯要結之時孰不謂必盟而後定哉
兹惟相諭以言相信以心東州有命齊無所虞
也北州有命衛無所疑也視盟詛煩而亂是用
長者不有間耶噫講信脩睦之道尚矣春秋之
世乃有不盟而交孚如齊衛者寧非隆古之遺
風哉故特書胥命著其善也召陵何盟齊桓退
punctuated:
《春秋》
「夏，齊侯、衛侯胥命于蒲」〔桓公三年〕，「楚屈完來盟于師，盟于召陵」〔僖公四年〕。
成以蒙
同考試官教諭謝　批：〔詞雅詞峻，且發聖人不貴盟戰意，委曲詳盡，可以式矣。〕
考試官教諭王　批：〔嚴整瑩潔。〕
考試官教諭趙　批：〔詞調雄渾。〕
以信相諭者，《春秋》善之；以禮服遠者，《春秋》美之。此蒲之信、召陵之禮，均爲近於古也。且于蒲何命？齊、衛以牧伯相推也。《春秋》善之者何？蓋信以發志，信不足而從事于盟，風之所以日漓也。矧齊、衛當兩伯要結之時，孰不謂必盟而後定哉？兹惟相諭以言，相信以心。東州有命，齊無所虞也；北州有命，衛無所疑也。視盟詛煩而亂是用長者，不有間耶？噫！講信脩睦之道尚矣，《春秋》之世乃有不盟而交孚如齊、衛者，寧非隆古之遺風哉？故特書「胥命」，著其善也。召陵何盟？齊桓退…
translation_en:
The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

"In summer, the Marquis of Qi and the Marquis of Wei exchanged charges at Pu" [3rd year of Duke Huan]; "Qu Wan of Chu came to covenant with the army, and covenanted at Shaoling" [4th year of Duke Xi].

By Cheng Yimeng 成以蒙.

Associate Examiner Instructor (jiaoyu) Xie 謝 comments: [The diction is elegant and incisive; moreover, it brings out the Sage's intent in not valuing covenants or warfare, in a nuanced and thorough manner that can serve as a model.]
Examiner Instructor Wang 王 comments: [Rigorous, orderly, luminous, and pure.]
Examiner Instructor Zhao 趙 comments: [The phrasing and cadence are vigorous and profound.]

When states come to mutual understanding through good faith, the Spring and Autumn Annals approves of them; when they win over the distant through ritual propriety, the Spring and Autumn Annals praises them. Thus the good faith at Pu and the ritual propriety at Shaoling were both close to antiquity.

Now, what was the charge at Pu? Qi and Wei deferred to one another as regional overlords. Why did the Spring and Autumn Annals approve of this? Because good faith gives expression to intent; when good faith is insufficient and rulers resort to covenants, that is why customs grow daily more debased. How much more so when Qi and Wei were in an era when the two overlords were binding each other by pacts—who would not have said that stability could only be achieved after swearing a covenant? Yet here they reached mutual understanding through words alone and trusted one another in their hearts. When the eastern region had a charge, Qi had nothing to worry about; when the northern region had a charge, Wei had nothing to doubt. Compared to those whose covenants and curses grew frequent and thereby fostered disorder, is there not a great difference? Alas! The Way of cultivating good faith and promoting harmony is of remote antiquity. That in the age of the Spring and Autumn Annals there were states like Qi and Wei that trusted each other without swearing a covenant—was this not a surviving custom of high antiquity? Therefore it specially records "exchanged charges" (xuming) to make manifest their goodness.

What was the covenant at Shaoling? Huan of Qi withdrew…

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
師以禮楚也春秋美之者何蓋招攜以禮禮不
足而相尋於兵亂之所以日滋也矧齊桓於師
強敵服之餘孰有不求快於一逞哉茲惟綏以
文德臨以持重斂厚積之衆而退舍以避之也
即喙息之餘而同好以徼之也視兵不戢而殘
民以逞者不有間耶噫舞干因壘之化邈矣春
秋之世乃有不戰而屈人如齊桓者寧非末世
之僅見哉故特書來盟序其績也夫重信則民
不疑重禮則民不爭聖人經世之意深哉雖然
齊衛信矣而桃丘之遇卒以詐魯召陵善矣而
伐陳之役驕溢漸滋焉以是知伯功之假不足
以語不息之誠也春秋與之姑以垂世教也學
者尚合而觀之
===
公會晉侯宋公陳侯衛侯鄭伯曹伯莒子
邾子滕子薛伯齊世子光吳人鄫人于
戚〔襄公五年〕
呂柟
同考試官教諭謝 批〔進吳所以遵中國經義則然是〕
punctuated:
師以禮楚也。《春秋》美之者何？蓋招攜以禮，禮不足而相尋於兵，亂之所以日滋也。矧齊桓於師強敵服之餘，孰有不求快於一逞哉？茲惟綏以文德，臨以持重，斂厚積之衆，而退舍以避之也；即喙息之餘，而同好以徼之也。視兵不戢而殘民以逞者，不有間耶？噫！舞干因壘之化邈矣，《春秋》之世，乃有不戰而屈人如齊桓者，寧非末世之僅見哉？故特書「來盟」，序其績也。夫重信則民不疑，重禮則民不爭，聖人經世之意深哉！雖然，齊、衛信矣，而桃丘之遇，卒以詐魯；召陵善矣，而伐陳之役，驕溢漸滋焉。以是知伯功之假，不足以語不息之誠也。《春秋》與之，姑以垂世教也，學者尚合而觀之。

「公會晉侯、宋公、陳侯、衛侯、鄭伯、曹伯、莒子、邾子、滕子、薛伯、齊世子光、吳人、鄫人于戚。」〔襄公五年〕
呂柟
同考試官教諭謝批：〔進吳所以遵中國，經義則然。是〕
translation_en:
… his army in order to treat Chu with propriety. Why did the Spring and Autumn Annals praise this? It is because one wins over the estranged through ritual propriety; when ritual propriety is insufficient and states resort repeatedly to arms against one another, disorder grows daily. Moreover, after Duke Huan of Qi had assembled a mighty army and forced the enemy to submit, who would not have sought the gratification of unleashing a single decisive strike? Yet here he pacified them through civil virtue and approached them with measured restraint, holding back his heavily massed troops and retreating a stage to yield to them, and meeting those who were barely catching their breath by seeking shared amity with them. Compared with those who fail to lay down their weapons and brutalize the people to satisfy their ambitions, is there not a vast difference? Alas! Far off indeed was the transforming influence of dancing with shields and making use of existing ramparts! That in the age of the Spring and Autumn there was someone like Duke Huan of Qi who subdued others without fighting—was this not a rare sight in a degenerate age? Therefore it specially recorded "came to covenant" in order to set forth his achievement. Now, when trustworthiness is valued, the people do not doubt; when ritual propriety is valued, the people do not contend. Profound indeed was the sage's intent in ordering the world! Even so, Qi and Wei showed trustworthiness, yet in the meeting at Taoqiu they ended up deceiving Lu; Shaoling was admirable, yet in the campaign against Chen, arrogance and excess gradually grew. From this we know that the borrowed virtue of hegemonic achievements is unworthy to be spoken of alongside unceasing sincerity. The Spring and Autumn Annals granted them approval provisionally so as to hand down a lesson for the world; scholars ought to examine them together.

"The Duke met the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Earl of Cao, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, Heir Apparent Guang of Qi, a man of Wu, and a man of Zeng at Qi." [5th year of Duke Xiang]
Lü Nan
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Xie: [Promoting Wu was a means of honoring the Central States; the meaning of the Classic is indeed thus. This …]

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
作直揭其旨而詞復謹嚴乃錄之
考試官教諭王　批　〔銘鑄左史〕
考試官教諭趙　批　〔體醇骨勁〕
遠人慕義以脩好春秋特進之也此吳人來會
而不爲主春秋善之其重內抑外之微意歟且
于戚何會吳請脩好而晉合諸侯以會之也夫
僭王之吳經嘗舉號以黜之矣茲何以稱人曰
太伯肇吳實宗盟之裔胄也貶而黜之則罪有
可懲者耳今也慕晉伯之方隆乃革心以向化
===
始有聽好之請則壽越遣焉無敢抗也繼聞會
期之徵則善道從焉無敢逆也夫會請于吳則
是仗義在晉而慕義在吳其志旣可尙已會徵
于晉則是制命在晉而從命在吳其分未始瀆
也嗚呼吳自伐郯以來其憑凌上國屢矣乃今
斂强大之勢而降心相從則事殊於夷不得復
以夷禮待之也吳自鍾離以來其狎主諸侯舊
矣乃今易爭雄之習而戢志推先則事同中國
不得不以中國之禮待之也故特進而稱人予
punctuated:
作直揭其旨，而詞復謹嚴，乃錄之。
考試官教諭王批〔銘鑄左史〕。
考試官教諭趙批〔體醇骨勁〕。
遠人慕義以脩好，《春秋》特進之也。此吳人來會而不爲主，《春秋》善之，其重內抑外之微意歟？且于戚，何會？吳請脩好，而晉合諸侯以會之也。夫僭王之吳，經嘗舉號以黜之矣，茲何以稱人？曰：太伯肇吳，實宗盟之裔胄也。貶而黜之，則罪有可懲者耳。今也慕晉伯之方隆，乃革心以向化。始有聽好之請，則壽越遣焉，無敢抗也；繼聞會期之徵，則善道從焉，無敢逆也。夫會請于吳，則是仗義在晉，而慕義在吳，其志旣可尙已；會徵于晉，則是制命在晉，而從命在吳，其分未始瀆也。嗚呼！吳自伐郯以來，其憑凌上國屢矣。乃今斂强大之勢，而降心相從，則事殊於夷，不得復以夷禮待之也。吳自鍾離以來，其狎主諸侯舊矣。乃今易爭雄之習，而戢志推先，則事同中國，不得不以中國之禮待之也。故特進而稱人，予
translation_en:
… essay directly unveils the essential meaning, and its phrasing is moreover rigorous and disciplined; therefore, it has been selected for inclusion.
Examiner and Instructor Wang comments: [Cast and molded in the style of the Zuo Commentary and historical records.]
Examiner and Instructor Zhao comments: [Pure in form and vigorous in structure.]
When distant peoples admire righteousness and seek to cultivate friendly relations, the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) specially elevates them. Here, the people of Wu came to the covenant meeting without acting as its host; the Spring and Autumn Annals commends this—is this not its subtle intent of honoring the interior states and restraining the exterior ones? Moreover, regarding the meeting at Qi, what sort of meeting was it? Wu requested to cultivate friendly relations, and Jin assembled the feudal lords to meet with them. Now, as for Wu, which usurped the title of king, the Classic had previously referred to it merely by its state name in order to degrade it; why, then, is it here termed "people" (ren)? It may be said: Taibo founded Wu, so it is truly a descendant lineage of the royal house's covenant. When it was disparaged and degraded, it was merely because it had offenses that required reprimand. Now, admiring the flourishing hegemony of Jin, it reformed its heart to turn toward civilization. First, there was the request to attend to friendly relations, for which Shou Yue was dispatched, not daring to be defiant; subsequently, upon hearing the summons for the meeting date, it followed along at Shandao, not daring to be recalcitrant. Now, since the meeting was requested by Wu, upholding righteousness lay with Jin while admiring righteousness lay with Wu—its aspiration was already worthy of esteem; and since the meeting was summoned by Jin, issuing commands lay with Jin while obeying commands lay with Wu—its proper station was never violated. Alas! Ever since its campaign against Tan, Wu had repeatedly encroached upon and bullied the upper states. Yet now it restrained its mighty power and humbled its heart to follow along; thus its conduct differed from that of the barbarians, and it could no longer be treated according to barbarian rites. Ever since the meeting at Zhongli, Wu had long been accustomed to taking turns presiding over the feudal lords. Yet now it changed its habit of vying for supremacy, reined in its ambitions, and yielded precedence; thus its conduct was the same as that of the Central States, and it could not but be treated according to the rites of the Central States. Therefore, the Classic specially elevates it by calling it "people," granting approval…

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
之也予吳所以尊中國也而聖人重內抑外之
意不居然可見哉抑吳之强也亞臣道之也而
悼之伯也吳與有力焉若然則二國之交有由
然矣夫予於數會而一進之蓋取節焉者也卒
之黃池會而勢益張晉且聽命不遑矣詩云誰
生厲階至今爲梗吾於晉悼亦云
禮記
爵人於朝與士共之
萬自約
同考試官教諭侯　批〔發先王命爵之公意明暢透徹〕
===
〔且結歸養士探本之論也宜錄以式〕
考試官教諭王　批〔純順雅暢〕
考試官教諭趙　批〔贍整可讀〕
觀先王命德之典而大公之心見矣蓋公論每
定於朝廷也王者命德而必於是誼非所以示
大公也哉且爵賞天下之公器而舉賢士類之
公心吾觀先王之頒爵也既審擇其人矣而寵
命之隆錫之自公朝焉匪由內降也名位之重
punctuated:
之也。予吳所以尊中國也，而聖人重內抑外之意，不居然可見哉！抑吳之强也，亞臣道之也；而悼之伯也，吳與有力焉。若然，則二國之交，有由然矣。夫予於數會而一進之，蓋取節焉者也。卒之黃池會而勢益張，晉且聽命不遑矣。《詩》云：「誰生厲階，至今爲梗。」吾於晉悼亦云。

《禮記》
爵人於朝，與士共之。
萬自約
同考試官教諭侯　批〔發先王命爵之公意，明暢透徹，且結歸養士，探本之論也，宜錄以式。〕
考試官教諭王　批〔純順雅暢。〕
考試官教諭趙　批〔贍整可讀。〕

觀先王命德之典，而大公之心見矣。蓋公論每定於朝廷也，王者命德而必於是，誼非所以示大公也哉！且爵賞，天下之公器；而舉賢，士類之公心。吾觀先王之頒爵也，既審擇其人矣，而寵命之隆，錫之自公朝焉，匪由內降也；名位之重，
translation_en:
… praising it. Praising Wu is the means by which the Central States are honored, and can the Sage's intention of valuing the interior and restraining the exterior not readily be seen in this? Moreover, the rise of Wu's power was guided by Wuchen [? written 亞臣]; and in Duke Dao of Jin's attainment of hegemony, Wu had a hand in it. If this is so, then the alliance between the two states had its underlying reasons. That the Sage commended them across several covenants and once elevated Wu's status was simply a matter of approving a single point of conduct. In the end, by the time of the covenant at Huangchi, Wu's power grew even more rampant, and Jin barely had time to obey its commands. As the Book of Odes (Shi) says: "Who produced these steps of evil, which to this day are a distress?" I say the same of Duke Dao of Jin.

Record of Rites (Liji)
"Conferring ranks upon men in the court is sharing it with the officers."
Wan Ziyue 萬自約
Associate Examiner, Instructor Hou, comments: [He brings out the impartial intention behind the former kings' conferral of ranks clearly, fluently, and thoroughly; moreover, his conclusion returns to the nurturing of officers—an argument that probes the fundamental root. It should be recorded as a model.]
Examiner, Instructor Wang, comments: [Pure, smooth, elegant, and fluent.]
Examiner, Instructor Zhao, comments: [Rich, well-ordered, and worth reading.]

When we observe the canonical statute by which the former kings gave charge to the virtuous, their mind of great impartiality becomes evident. For public opinion is always settled at the royal court; when a true king gives charge to the virtuous and unfailingly does so there, is the principle not to display great impartiality? Furthermore, ranks and rewards are the public instruments of the world, while recommending the worthy is the public mind of the scholarly class. When I observe how the former kings bestowed ranks, after they had carefully selected the men, the lofty favor of the charge was granted from the public court, not handed down privately from the inner palace; the weight of title and position…

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
定之自公朝焉不以私授也若是者何哉亦惟
與士共之而已蓋公朝士類之所聚而士類則
公論之所出者也故王者之官人行藝有辨則
爵之宜也顧登選之典不敢獨專於已而大廷
晉接之所寔簡畀之命所由出明試有徵則爵
之宜也顧進賢之道不可不同於人而庶明羣
集之地寔建德之舉所由行賢可庸也君行之
羣工成之雖制命在人君而未始不通乎衆志
覲明揚之盛者知師錫之有在也斯則天命有
德匪直一人作福之柄而已才可舉也上制之
多士從之雖駁貴在天子而未始不協夫輿情
覩觀光之會者知詢謀之僉同也斯則天職共
治不爲一人作好之私而已是知先王之舉賢
不惟擇之明而又行之公如此此朝無倖位而
享得人之慶也與抑用人固貴乎公而養士實
貴乎豫故成周造士之法若六禮七敎至纖悉
矣而得人之盛亙古一見焉使之不預預則雖
詳且公其與幾何然則育賢者其尚知所本云
punctuated: 定之自公朝焉，不以私授也。若是者何哉？亦惟與士共之而已。蓋公朝，士類之所聚；而士類，則公論之所出者也。故王者之官人，行藝有辨，則爵之宜也；顧登選之典，不敢獨專於已，而大廷晉接之所，寔簡畀之命所由出。明試有徵，則爵之宜也；顧進賢之道，不可不同於人，而庶明羣集之地，寔建德之舉所由行。賢可庸也，君行之，羣工成之，雖制命在人君，而未始不通乎衆志，覲明揚之盛者，知師錫之有在也，斯則天命有德，匪直一人作福之柄而已。才可舉也，上制之，多士從之，雖馭貴在天子，而未始不協夫輿情，覩觀光之會者，知詢謀之僉同也，斯則天職共治，不爲一人作好之私而已。是知先王之舉賢，不惟擇之明，而又行之公如此，此朝無倖位，而享得人之慶也與！抑用人固貴乎公，而養士實貴乎豫。故成周造士之法，若六禮、七敎，至纖悉矣，而得人之盛，亙古一見焉。使之不預預，則雖詳且公，其與幾何？然則育賢者，其尚知所本云。
translation_en:
… determined from the public court, and not bestowed out of private favor. Why is it like this? It is simply a matter of sharing it with the scholars. For the public court is where the scholarly class gathers, and the scholarly class is whence public opinion emerges.

Therefore, when a true king appoints men to office, once their conduct and arts have been distinguished, it is fitting to confer rank upon them. Yet he does not dare to monopolize the canon of selection and promotion for himself alone; rather, the place of audience in the great court is truly whence the mandate of selection and appointment issues. Once clear testing has yielded verification, it is fitting to confer rank upon them. Yet the way of advancing the worthy cannot but be shared with others; rather, the place where the enlightened multitude gathers is truly where the act of establishing the virtuous is carried out.

When the worthy are fit to be employed, the ruler enacts it and thesembled officials complete it. Although the power to issue commands rests with the sovereign, it never fails to communicate with the will of the multitude. Those who witness the splendor of open promotion know that the recommendations of the multitude have their basis. Thus Heaven charges the virtuous, and it is not merely the prerogative of one man alone to dispense blessings.

When the talented are fit to be elevated, the sovereign institutes it and the many scholars follow it. Although control over noble rank [reading 馭 for 駁] rests with the Son of Heaven, it never fails to harmonize with popular sentiment. Those who behold the gathering of state guests know that deliberations and counsels are unanimous. Thus the offices of Heaven are governed in common, and it is not merely the private partiality of one man indulging his personal preferences.

From this we know that in elevating the worthy, the former kings not only selected them with clarity, but also carried it out with such impartiality. Is this not why the court had no undeserved positions and enjoyed the blessing of obtaining the right men?

And yet, while employing men certainly prizes impartiality, nurturing scholars truly prizes prior preparation. Thus the methods of the flourishing Zhou for cultivating scholars—such as the Six Rites and Seven Teachings—were thorough to the utmost detail, and the abundance of talent it obtained has been seen but once in all antiquity. Had they not been prepared in advance [?], then even if selection were detailed and impartial, how many could have been approved? Therefore, may those who nurture the worthy still know where the root lies.

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
論倫無患樂之情也欣喜歡愛樂之官也
中正無邪禮之質也莊敬恭順禮之制
也
陳震
同考試官教諭李　批〔禮樂情官質制講者易浮靡此〕
篇切實明暢可與言禮樂者
考試官教諭王　批〔明順整飭〕
考試官教諭趙　批〔詳而有體〕
記者詳言禮樂之義有屬之理者有屬之人者
===
蓋情與質禮樂之本然而官與制則人之用禮
樂者也知斯義也而禮樂其可興乎樂記之意
蓋曰禮樂之在天下非可以私意創爲之也蓋
有深意存焉而不明其義者難語制作之精矣
何則樂以宣和必有情也情豈聲音之謂哉詩
言志而足論律和聲而有倫雍雍乎浤滯之不
形非樂之本情乎人心則有無聲之樂焉性眞
適而欣喜之自如也天機暢而歡愛之交通也
則太和在吾心而聲氣之元已得由是咏詩歌
punctuated:
「論倫無患，樂之情也；欣喜歡愛，樂之官也。中正無邪，禮之質也；莊敬恭順，禮之制也。」

陳震

同考試官教諭李　批：〔禮樂情官質制，講者易浮靡，此〕篇切實明暢，可與言禮樂者。
考試官教諭王　批：〔明順整飭。〕
考試官教諭趙　批：〔詳而有體。〕

記者詳言禮樂之義，有屬之理者，有屬之人者。蓋情與質，禮樂之本然；而官與制，則人之用禮樂者也。知斯義也，而禮樂其可興乎！《樂記》之意，蓋曰：禮樂之在天下，非可以私意創爲之也，蓋有深意存焉，而不明其義者，難語制作之精矣。何則？樂以宣和，必有情也。情豈聲音之謂哉？詩言志而足論，律和聲而有倫，雍雍乎浤滯之不形，非樂之本情乎？人心則有無聲之樂焉：性眞適而欣喜之自如也，天機暢而歡愛之交通也。則太和在吾心，而聲氣之元已得，由是咏詩歌、
translation_en:
"Discussing order without discord is the inner reality of music; delight, joy, gladness, and affection are the functional offices of music. Impartiality, rectitude, and freedom from perversity are the essential substance of ritual; gravity, reverence, respectfulness, and compliance are the regulative measures of ritual."

Chen Zhen 陳震

Associate Examiner and Instructor Li 李 comments: 〔When expounding upon the inner reality, functional offices, essential substance, and regulative measures of ritual and music, commentators easily slip into superficiality and floridness; this〕 essay is substantive, clear, and fluent—one with whom ritual and music may truly be discussed.
Examiner and Instructor Wang 王 comments: 〔Lucid, smooth, and well-ordered.〕
Examiner and Instructor Zhao 趙 comments: 〔Detailed and well-structured.〕

The compiler of the Record sets forth in detail the meaning of ritual and music, distinguishing between that which pertains to principle and that which pertains to man. For inner reality and essential substance are the inherent nature of ritual and music, whereas functional offices and regulative measures are the means by which men put ritual and music into practice. Once one understands this meaning, can ritual and music not be made to flourish? The purport of the Record of Music (Yueji 樂記) is broadly this: ritual and music exist in the world not as things that can be fabricated out of private whim; rather, a profound meaning abides within them, and with one who does not grasp that meaning, it is difficult to speak of the subtlety of their creation and institution. Why is this so? Music serves to diffuse harmony, and thus it must possess an inner reality. Yet how could this inner reality merely refer to sounds and tones? Poetry expresses intent so that it suffices for discourse, and the pitch-standards harmonize sounds so that they possess coherent order; harmoniously and serenely, no discordant obstruction [?] takes form—is this not the fundamental reality of music? In the human mind there is a soundless music: when one's true nature is at ease, delight and joy are spontaneous; when the heavenly mechanism flows freely, gladness and affection communicate with one another. Thus supreme harmony resides within one's own mind, and the primal source of sound and vital breath is already attained; from this, when one chants poetry and songs, …

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
調律品所謂諭倫者殆管攝於是矣苟無其官
作樂之主亡矣其如樂何禮以辨序必有質也
質豈度數之謂哉行之中而無過不及立之正
而無所偏倚秩秩乎邪僻之不作非禮之本質
乎人身則有無體之禮焉主之嚴肅而儼乎其
莊敬也持之退讓而巽然其恭順也則至序在
吾心而秩敘之精已具由是觀會通行典禮所
謂中正者蓋宰制於是矣苟無其制行禮之本
失矣其如禮何夫樂得其官則大樂所由興而
===
聖人作之以應天者此也禮得其制則大禮所
由立而聖人制之以配地者此也其意義之深
夫豈人之易識也哉抑聞之心思不通乎性命
不足以言禮樂則禮樂之義誠未可以易言也
三代而後律品之爭在累黍長短之閒而禮經
出漢儒之附會則三千三百存十一焉耳非特
義不可知而數亦未易陳矣然則有志興禮樂
者性命之學可勿之講乎
第貳場
punctuated:
調律品，所謂「諭倫」者，殆管攝於是矣。苟無其官，作樂之主亡矣，其如樂何！禮以辨序，必有質也，質豈度數之謂哉？行之中而無過不及，立之正而無所偏倚，秩秩乎邪僻之不作，非禮之本質乎？人身則有無體之禮焉。主之嚴肅而儼乎其莊敬也，持之退讓而巽然其恭順也，則至序在吾心，而秩敘之精已具。由是觀會通、行典禮，所謂「中正」者，蓋宰制於是矣。苟無其制，行禮之本失矣，其如禮何！夫樂得其官，則大樂所由興，而聖人作之以應天者此也；禮得其制，則大禮所由立，而聖人制之以配地者此也。其意義之深，夫豈人之易識也哉？抑聞之：心思不通乎性命，不足以言禮樂。則禮樂之義，誠未可以易言也。三代而後，律品之爭在累黍長短之閒，而禮經出漢儒之附會，則三千三百存十一焉耳。非特義不可知，而數亦未易陳矣。然則有志興禮樂者，性命之學可勿之講乎？
第貳場
translation_en:
…and harmonizing the pitch-pipes, what is called "making clear the human relationships without falsehood" is virtually encompassed right here. If it lacks this governing office, the presiding principle of creating music is lost—what then can one do with music? Ritual serves to distinguish order, so it must have its substance; yet how could substance merely mean measures and numbers? Practicing the mean without excess or deficiency, standing in rectitude without partiality or leaning, so orderly that perversity and depravity do not arise—is this not the essential substance of ritual? Within the human person, then, there is a bodiless ritual. When one presides over it with solemnity, how dignified is one's grave reverence! When one maintains it with謙yielding, how compliant is one's respectful obedience! Then supreme order resides in one's own mind, and the essence of ranked arrangement is already complete. From this, one observes the convergence and continuity of things and carries out the canonical rites; what is called "centrality and rectitude" is indeed governed and regulated right here. If it lacks this regulation, the root of practicing ritual is lost—what then can one do with ritual? Now, when music attains its governing office, that is whereby Great Music arises, and it is by this that the sages created it to respond to Heaven; when ritual attains its regulation, that is whereby Great Ritual is established, and it is by this that the sages instituted it to match Earth. As for the profundity of their meaning and significance, how could it be easily understood by people? Moreover, I have heard it said: if the thoughts of one's mind do not penetrate human nature and Heaven's decree, one is not qualified to speak of ritual and music. Thus, the significance of ritual and music truly cannot be spoken of lightly. After the Three Dynasties, disputes over the pitch-pipes centered on the length of stacked millet grains, while the ritual classics emerged from the strained interpretations of Han scholars, so that of the three thousand and three hundred rules, barely one in ten survived. Not only can their deeper meaning no longer be known, even their technical numbers are not easy to set forth. This being so, for those who aspire to revive ritual and music, can the learning of human nature and Heaven's decree go unstudied?

Second Session

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
論
明主游心帝王之術
施重光
同考試官教諭李　批〔以定志立論得漢臣進言之意至命詞遣調則寓馴於奇摛藻以雅論之傑出者宜錄以式〕
考試官教諭王　批〔駕衡凌向當是作家〕
考試官教諭趙　批〔古雅醇正〕
人主之心必有所用知所以善其用則志定而
天下之治成何則人主惟一心天下之可願欲
而紛然並馳則此心且不爲我有何以爲治故
其道在擇術術者定志之具而適治之路也是
故明主先焉孳孳問學誦法古昔行帝道而帝
行王道而王自我決之而已矣明主游心帝王
===
者安極而其勢又無不得於天下使中無所擇
之術漢張敞爲宣帝言也背謂人主一身天所
大奉四海九州梯航篚篚之物足以供服御離
宮別苑參副之乘甲乙之帳足以待宴遊左右
贅御才智技巧勇力之倫足以奉指使凡天下
punctuated:
論
明主游心帝王之術
施重光
同考試官教諭李　批：〔以定志立論，得漢臣進言之意。至命詞遣調，則寓馴於奇，摛藻以雅，論之傑出者，宜錄以式。〕
考試官教諭王　批：〔駕衡凌向，當是作家。〕
考試官教諭趙　批：〔古雅醇正。〕
人主之心必有所用。知所以善其用，則志定而天下之治成。何則？人主惟一心，天下之可願欲、而紛然並馳，則此心且不爲我有，何以爲治？故其道在擇術。術者，定志之具而適治之路也。是故明主先焉。孳孳問學，誦法古昔，行帝道而帝，行王道而王，自我決之而已矣。「明主游心帝王、者安極？而其勢又無不得於天下。使中無所擇、之術」，漢張敞爲宣帝言也。背謂人主一身，天所大奉，四海九州梯航篚篚之物，足以供服御；離宮別苑、參副之乘、甲乙之帳，足以待宴遊；左右贅御、才智技巧勇力之倫，足以奉指使。凡天下
translation_en:
Discourse

"An Enlightened Ruler Directs His Mind to the Arts of the Five Emperors and Three Kings"

Shi Chongguang 施重光

Associate Examiner and Confucian Instructor Li 李 comments: [Establishing his argument on fixing the ruler's will, he grasps the intent of the Han minister's remonstrance. As for his choice of words and tone, he lodges smoothness within originality and unfolds elegance with refinement. This is an outstanding discourse and ought to be recorded as a model.]

Examiner and Confucian Instructor Wang 王 comments: [Surpassing Kuang Heng 匡衡 and outstripping Liu Xiang 劉向, he must be a master writer.]

Examiner and Confucian Instructor Zhao 趙 comments: [Classically elegant, pure, and upright.]

The mind of a ruler must be applied to something. If he knows how to apply it well, his will becomes fixed and the governance of all under Heaven is accomplished. Why is this? A ruler possesses but a single mind, whereas where do the desirable things in the world have any limit? Moreover, by his position there is nothing in the world he cannot obtain. If within himself he has nothing to guide his choice, and his desires gallop forth in confused array, then this mind will not even remain his own possession—how then could he achieve good governance? Therefore, the proper way lies in choosing one's art. An art is the instrument for fixing the will and the road that leads to order; for this reason, an enlightened ruler puts it first. Diligently inquiring and learning, reciting and modeling himself upon antiquity—practicing the Way of the Five Emperors to become an Emperor, or practicing the Way of the Three Kings to become a King—this is simply decided by oneself alone.

"An enlightened ruler directs his mind to the arts of the Five Emperors and Three Kings"—this was spoken by Zhang Chang 張敞 of the Han dynasty for Emperor Xuan 宣帝. I have privately considered [?] that the ruler's own person is grandly provided for by Heaven: the tribute brought in baskets by scaling mountains and sailing seas from the Four Seas and Nine Provinces is sufficient to supply his clothing and personal use; detached palaces and separate parks, attendant and auxiliary carriages, and curtains of the first and second grades are sufficient to await his banquets and excursions; close attendants [?] around him and men of talent, wisdom, skill, and bravery are sufficient to obey his beck and call. Of all that in the world… [Note: columns 9 and 10 of this page appear swapped in the woodblock transcription; the translation restores their syntactic order.]

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
之可願欲者無不可得獨以爲不可致者神不
可知者年耳而儇人媚子伺間投隙又爲之嚮
導於外究其所爲不至車轍馬迹周行天下騁
望琅邪之臺佇想蓬萊之丘未已也甚矣術之
不可不審也冀北越南跬步千里審得其術則
心逸而有餘審失其術則心勞而不足人主奈
何舍逸而取勞去有餘而就不足也彼厭崇高
富厚從事於方外以幾長生豈不以爲至愉快
也及其焦神極能竟如景響不可得假令得之
===
必且遺世獨立如山林枯槁之爲人主何慕焉
然而快於此者不察故也當其不察而徒曰此
非明主之所宜爲何以奪其所嚮往使憣然改
圖蓋有術焉以易之自古及今言治理者孰不
曰二帝三王夫帝王之術非天降地出由人心
生者也嘗誦二氏之典謨稽三代之載籍得其
所爲術者精一執中時雍風動唐虞所以肇帝
功也祇台平成懋昭表正緝熙新命作求成乎
夏后殷周所以開王業也此皆本於身心施於
punctuated: 之可願欲者，無不可得，獨以爲不可致者神，不可知者年耳。而儇人媚子伺間投隙，又爲之嚮導於外。究其所爲，不至車轍馬迹周行天下，騁望琅邪之臺，佇想蓬萊之丘，未已也。甚矣，術之不可不審也！冀北越南，跬步千里。審得其術，則心逸而有餘；審失其術，則心勞而不足。人主奈何舍逸而取勞，去有餘而就不足也？彼厭崇高富厚，從事於方外以幾長生，豈不以爲至愉快也？及其焦神極能，竟如景響不可得。假令得之，必且遺世獨立，如山林枯槁之爲，人主何慕焉？然而快於此者，不察故也。當其不察，而徒曰「此非明主之所宜爲」，何以奪其所嚮往，使憣然改圖？蓋有術焉以易之。自古及今，言治理者，孰不曰二帝三王？夫帝王之術，非天降地出，由人心生者也。嘗誦二氏之典謨，稽三代之載籍，得其所爲術者。精一執中，時雍風動，唐、虞所以肇帝功也；祇台平成，懋昭表正，緝熙新命，作求成乎，夏后、殷、周所以開王業也。此皆本於身心，施於
translation_en: …that might be wished for or desired cannot be obtained; he thinks only that what cannot be summoned are the spirits, and what cannot be known is the span of his years. Then agile flatterers and fawning minions watch for openings and exploit crevices, acting besides as his guides on the outside. If we trace what he does to the end, until his chariot ruts and horse tracks have circled the realm, until he has gazed afar from the terrace of Langye and stood longing for the hills of Penglai, he will not stop! How extreme is the need to examine one's art carefully! Between north toward Ji and south toward Yue, a half-step leads to a divergence of a thousand li. If upon examination one attains the right art, the mind is at ease and has abundance; if one misses the art, the mind toils and is left in want. Why ever would a ruler of men cast aside ease to take up toil, or abandon abundance to pursue want? When those rulers grow weary of exalted status and rich abundance, and busy themselves with transcendent realms outside the world in hopes of longevity, do they not consider this the ultimate delight? Yet when they have scorched their spirit and exhausted their faculties, in the end it is like chasing shadows and echoes, impossible to obtain. And even supposing they did obtain it, they would have to forsake the world and stand alone, acting like withered hermits in the mountains and forests—what is there in that for a ruler of men to admire? Yet the reason they take delight in such things is a lack of discernment. While a ruler fails to discern this, if one merely says, "This is not what an enlightened ruler ought to do," how can that wrest away his yearning and cause him to turn about and change his plans? There must be an art with which to replace it. From antiquity to the present, among those who speak of the principles of governance, who does not speak of the Two Emperors and Three Kings? Now the art of the Emperors and Kings does not drop from Heaven or spring from the earth; it is born from the human mind. I have recited the canons and counsels of the Two Clauses [Yao and Shun] and examined the records of the Three Dynasties, and found what constituted their art. "Refined and single-minded, holding fast to the Mean," bringing harmony to the times and moving the people like the wind—this is how Tang [Yao] and Yu [Shun] initiated the achievements of Emperors. "Reverent in oneself," bringing peace and order; "striving to make bright virtue," setting up a standard of rectitude; "continuing bright illumination" to renew the Mandate and acting to seek completion in sincerity [?]—this is how the Lord of Xia, Yin [Shang], and Zhou founded the enterprises of Kings. All of these are rooted in the person and mind, and extended to…

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
天下國家以俟聖人於百世如夏葛而冬裘渴
飲而饑食也切而不可離也如規矩之於方圓
準繩之於平直也至而不可加也是故明主游
心焉夫人主之學不與衆庶同帝王往矣考信
六藝自齊魯諸儒猶或難之況人主乎蓋非欲
其貫數守墨以資博洽也亦非欲其含英泝潤
以資辭章也游心焉耳矣語稱游藝記稱息游
要以寄寓志意運用精神日玩索焉而不厭帝
王之術庸主之所疑畏明主之所嘉樂也故心
===
一也所游殊方與其游心萬里之外焦神極能
而無益於得孰與游二三策之中設誠致行可
使還至而立有效也故誦其言如親其人考其
事如當其世以吾之心合古帝王之心而渙然
釋怡然順焉此之謂游自古帝王蓋有不出戶
而知星辰不下堂而知山川不越階序而知政
俗者明目達聰也非以車馬也享國久延祚長
聲施至今者清心寡欲約己厚民也非以方術
也故目不廢玄黃黼黻之觀而無亂色耳不廢
punctuated: 天下國家，以俟聖人於百世。如夏葛而冬裘，渴飲而饑食也，切而不可離也；如規矩之於方圓，準繩之於平直也，至而不可加也。是故明主游心焉。夫人主之學，不與衆庶同。帝王往矣，考信六藝，自齊、魯諸儒猶或難之，況人主乎？蓋非欲其貫數守墨以資博洽也，亦非欲其含英泝潤以資辭章也，游心焉耳矣。《語》稱「游藝」，《記》稱「息游」，要以寄寓志意，運用精神，日玩索焉而不厭。帝王之術，庸主之所疑畏，明主之所嘉樂也。故心一也，所游殊方。與其游心萬里之外，焦神極能而無益於得，孰與游二三策之中，設誠致行，可使還至而立有效也？故誦其言如親其人，考其事如當其世，以吾之心合古帝王之心，而渙然釋、怡然順焉，此之謂游。自古帝王蓋有不出戶而知星辰，不下堂而知山川，不越階序而知政俗者，明目達聰也，非以車馬也；享國久、延祚長、聲施至今者，清心寡欲，約己厚民也，非以方術也。故目不廢玄黃黼黻之觀而無亂色，耳不廢
translation_en:
… the realm, the state, and the family, and may await a sage a hundred generations hence without doubt. They are like fine linen in summer and furs in winter, like drinking when thirsty and eating when hungry—so essential to human life that one cannot depart from them. They are like the compass and square in relation to circles and squares, or the level and plumb-line in relation to flatness and straightness—so supreme that nothing can be added to them. Therefore, the enlightened ruler lets his mind roam in them.

Now, the learning of a ruler of men is not the same as that of the multitude. The emperors and kings of antiquity are gone; verifying the truth through the Six Arts was something that even the various scholars of Qi and Lu sometimes found difficult—how much more so a ruler of men? For the aim is not to have him master numerology and cleave to ink and line in order to furnish broad erudition, nor is it to have him savor blossoms and trace moisture in order to furnish literary composition; it is simply to let his mind roam in them. The Analects (Lunyu) speaks of "roaming in the arts," and the Record of Rites (Liji) speaks of "resting and roaming"; in essence, this means lodging one's aspirations and intentions there, exercising one's spirit, and contemplating and exploring them daily without tiring. The art of the emperors and kings is what mediocre rulers doubt and fear, yet what enlightened rulers admire and delight in.

Thus, the mind is one, yet the directions in which it roams differ. Rather than letting the mind roam ten thousand li away, exhausting one's spirit and taxing one's abilities to the utmost with no benefit to what is gained, how much better to roam within two or three bamboo slips of the classics, establishing sincerity and carrying them out in practice, whereby results can be made to arrive swiftly and take effect immediately? Therefore, reciting their words as though meeting the men in person, examining their deeds as though living in their age, joining one's own mind with the minds of the ancient emperors and kings until doubts dissolve and all becomes joyful and harmonious—this is what is meant by "roaming."

Since antiquity, among the emperors and kings there were indeed those who knew the stars and constellations without stepping out the door, knew the mountains and rivers without descending from the hall, and knew governance and customs without crossing the steps and walls; this was through clarifying their vision and extending their hearing, not through chariots and horses. That they enjoyed the realm for a long time, prolonged their dynastic fortune, and had their renown extend down to the present was through purifying their minds and lessening their desires, restraining themselves and being generous to the people, not through esoteric arts. Therefore, their eyes did not abandon the sight of black and yellow robes and embroidered emblems, yet there were no licentious sights; their ears did not abandon…

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
笙鏞鞉管之聽而無姦聲身不廢靈臺囿沼辟
雝之樂而無愆禮歲時不廢巡守省邁墮山翕
河之行而無淫游夫帝王之術豈迂闊而遠於
人情乎是故明主游心焉且人主之所好尚羣
下之所趨赴也好車馬則周秦耄荒之說中好
方術則燕齊迂怪之說中誠使移車馬方術之
好以好問學慕帝王而顧無帝臣王佐持唐虞
三代興理致平之術以中吾君者哉甚矣術之
不可不審也觀日月而知列宿之微也測江海
===
而知衆流之細也游心帝王而知百家之陋也
故法圖信史參列左右則梯航筐篚之物輕矣
疑丞輔弼賓友後先則左右儇媚之倫疎矣廣
廈細旃從容朝夕則駕乘供帳苑囿之娛末矣
由是觀之帝王之術與外物之好異端之說此
詘則彼信明主超然遠覽慓然獨悟心所嚮往
不在彼而在此是其擇術審而用志定也及其
成也羣生和百嘉鬯風雨節寒暑時三光常明
四靈畢至躋一世於仁壽之域豈獨其身長生
punctuated: 笙鏞鞉管之聽，而無姦聲；身不廢靈臺、囿沼、辟雝之樂，而無愆禮；歲時不廢巡守省邁、墮山翕河之行，而無淫游。夫帝王之術，豈迂闊而遠於人情乎？是故明主游心焉。且人主之所好尚，羣下之所趨赴也。好車馬，則周、秦耄荒之說中；好方術，則燕、齊迂怪之說中。誠使移車馬、方術之好以好問學、慕帝王，而顧無帝臣、王佐持唐、虞、三代興理致平之術以中吾君者哉！甚矣，術之不可不審也！觀日月而知列宿之微也，測江海而知衆流之細也，游心帝王而知百家之陋也。故法圖、信史參列左右，則梯航、筐篚之物輕矣；疑、丞、輔、弼、賓、友後先，則左右儇媚之倫疎矣；廣廈細旃，從容朝夕，則駕乘、供帳、苑囿之娛末矣。由是觀之，帝王之術，與外物之好、異端之說，此詘則彼信。明主超然遠覽，慓然獨悟，心所嚮往，不在彼而在此，是其擇術審而用志定也。及其成也，羣生和，百嘉鬯，風雨節，寒暑時，三光常明，四靈畢至，躋一世於仁壽之域，豈獨其身長生…
translation_en:
…listening to reed organs, large bells, hand-drums, and flutes, yet there were no licentious sounds; in their own persons they did not dispense with the pleasures of the Spirit Tower, parks, ponds, and the Hall of the Circular Moat (Biyong), yet there were no transgressions against ritual propriety; and at the seasonal times of the year they did not dispense with tours of inspection and royal progresses across the high mountains and the great rivers, yet there were no dissolute excursions. How could the art of the emperors and kings be impractical and remote from human feelings? Therefore, enlightened rulers let their minds roam within it.

Moreover, whatever the sovereign favors and esteems is what all his subordinates hasten to pursue. If he favors carriages and horses, then tales of the senile excesses of Zhou and Qin will hit the mark with him; if he favors esoteric arts, then the absurd and strange doctrines of Yan and Qi will hit the mark with him. If indeed he were to shift his fondness for carriages, horses, and esoteric arts toward a fondness for inquiry and learning and an admiration for the ancient emperors and kings, how could there fail to be imperial ministers and kingly aides holding forth the arts by which Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties fostered order and achieved peace so as to hit the mark with our sovereign! Profound indeed is the need to examine one's art with care! By beholding the sun and moon, one knows the dimness of the constellations; by sounding the Yangzi and the seas, one knows the pettiness of the myriad streams; by letting one's mind roam among the ancient emperors and kings, one knows the vulgarity of the Hundred Schools. Thus, when model diagrams and trustworthy histories are arrayed to his left and right, tributary goods brought by scaling mountains and sailing seas in baskets and hampers become of slight account; when the Four Advisors (yi, cheng, fu, bi), guests, and friends attend him before and behind, theagile flatterers about him are kept at a distance; when in spacious halls upon fine felt rugs he deliberates at leisure morning and evening, the amusements of carriages, palanquins, canopies, and hunting parks become trivialities. Viewed in this light, as between the art of the emperors and kings on the one hand, and the fondness for external things and heterodox doctrines on the other, when the one is bent back, the other extends forward. An enlightened ruler looks far ahead with transcendent detachment and awakens alone with keen swiftness; that toward which his heart inclines lies here and not there—this means that his choice of art is carefully examined and the application of his will is firmly settled. And when his achievement is complete, all living things are in harmony, the hundred blessings flourish, winds and rains are moderate, cold and heat come in their proper seasons, the three luminaries shine ever bright, the four numinous creatures all arrive, and he raises the entire age into the realm of benevolence and longevity—how could it merely be that his own person attains long life…

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
久視而已哉漢興於馬上不事詩書徒以節儉
休養四十餘年天下物力方盛而人主侈心亦
萌建元之間方士竝進車馬四出於是祠泰一
薦五時禮壽宮作甘泉桂觀庶幾安期羨門之
屬而海內耗矣宣帝因之復脩其故事令詞臣
建節遠求金馬碧雞而當世名儒號稱知學者
且獻淮南鴻寶苑祕之方帝之心駸駸乎武帝
之續矣夫表章六藝聚講石渠非不知有帝王
之術也而辨之不蚤故其志靡定而異說得乘
===
以入焉及一聞敞言悉罷上方待詔者此宣帝
之所以爲明也後世人主誠及車馬方士之好
未萌而審於擇術知所以游心焉則事半而功
倍此其明又過宣帝遠矣
表
擬以禮部左侍郎兼翰林院學士薛瑄從
祀孔子廟庭子孫謝表隆慶六年
楊俊臣
同考試官教諭莊　批〔敘文清從祀本末甚悉而立格〕
punctuated:
久視而已哉！漢興於馬上，不事《詩》、《書》，徒以節儉休養四十餘年，天下物力方盛，而人主侈心亦萌。建元之間，方士竝進，車馬四出，於是祠泰一，薦五時，禮壽宮，作甘泉、桂觀，庶幾安期、羨門之屬，而海內耗矣。宣帝因之，復脩其故事，令詞臣建節，遠求金馬、碧雞，而當世名儒號稱知學者，且獻淮南《鴻寶》、《苑祕》之方，帝之心駸駸乎武帝之續矣。夫表章六藝，聚講石渠，非不知有帝王之術也，而辨之不蚤，故其志靡定，而異說得乘以入焉。及一聞敞言，悉罷上方待詔者，此宣帝之所以爲明也。後世人主，誠及車馬、方士之好未萌，而審於擇術，知所以游心焉，則事半而功倍，此其明又過宣帝遠矣。

表
擬以禮部左侍郎兼翰林院學士薛瑄從祀孔子廟庭子孫謝表（隆慶六年）
楊俊臣
同考試官教諭莊　批〔敘文清從祀本末甚悉，而立格〕
translation_en:
…and enduring vision for his own person alone!

When the Han dynasty arose on horseback, it did not occupy itself with the Book of Odes (Shi) and the Book of Documents (Shu), but merely through frugality and recuperation for more than forty years, the material resources of the realm were just then at their height—and extravagant desires also sprouted in the ruler's heart. During the Jianyuan era (140–135 BCE), masters of esoterica (fangshi) advanced side by side and carriages and horses went out in all four directions. Thereupon the emperor sacrificed to the Supreme One (Taiyi), made offerings at the Five Altars (Wushi) [text reads 五時 for 五畤], performed rites at the Palace of Longevity (Shougong), and built the Sweet Springs Palace (Ganquan) and the Cinnamon Belvedere (Guiguan), hoping to encounter the likes of Anqi Sheng and Xianmen Gao—and the realm within the seas was exhausted. Emperor Xuan (Xuandi, r. 74–49 BCE) followed in turn and revived those precedents, ordering a literary official to bear imperial credentials and go afar in search of the Golden Horse (Jinma) and Jade Cock (Biji) spirits; meanwhile, a renowned Confucian scholar of the age, acclaimed as one who understood learning, even presented the Prince of Huainan's esoteric recipes of the Great Treasure (Hongbao) and Secret Garden (Yuanbi). The Emperor's mind was rapidly on its way to becoming a continuation of Emperor Wu's (Wudi, r. 141–87 BCE). Now, in exalting the Six Classics (Liuyi) and gathering scholars to lecture on them in the Stone Canal Pavilion (Shiqu ge), it was not that he did not know there existed the art of emperors and kings; yet because he did not discern this early on, his resolve was unsettled, and heterodox doctrines were able to take advantage of the opening to enter. Once he heard the words of Zhang Chang 張敞, however, he dismissed all the masters of recipes awaiting imperial edict (daizhao). This was why Emperor Xuan was considered enlightened. If rulers of later ages truly examine carefully their choice of art and know wherein to let their minds roam before a fondness for carriages, horses, and masters of esoterica has even sprouted, then with half the effort they will achieve twice the result, and their enlightenment will far surpass that of Emperor Xuan.

Memorial

Drafting a Memorial of Thanks on Behalf of the Descendants of Xue Xuan 薛瑄, Left Vice Minister of Rites (Libu zuo shilang) concurrently Hanlin Academician (Hanlinyuan xueshi), Upon His Enshrinement for Correlative Worship in the Temple Courtyard of Confucius (Sixth Year of Longqing [1572])

Yang Junchen 楊俊臣

Associate Examiner, Instructor (jiaoyu) Zhuang 莊, comment: 〔It recounts from beginning to end the enshrinement of Wenqing 文清 (Xue Xuan) in great detail, and in establishing its structure…〕

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
渾成搆詞典麗是閑於抽對者亟取之
考試官教諭王　批〔場中表不浮則宂此作根據磨　礱直歸大雅有宋人矩度〕
考試官教諭趙　批〔典則可誦〕
隆慶六年某月某日具官臣某伏蒙
聖恩以先臣禮部左侍郎兼翰林院學士薛瑄
從祀孔廟臣謹奉
表稱
謝者伏以
===
禮嚴祀事殊
恩下逮於先臣
道重儒林
曠典肇脩於
盛世議孚輿論裁自
宸衷榮溢薦紳感深末裔臣某誠懽誠忭稽首
頓首竊惟
先聖教垂夫萬世特廟酬功羣賢品列於四
科分庭侑食得其門者或寡非其類則不
punctuated:
〔渾成，搆詞典麗，是閑於抽對者。亟取之。〕
考試官教諭王批：〔場中表不浮則宂。此作根據磨礱，直歸大雅，有宋人矩度。〕
考試官教諭趙批：〔典則可誦。〕

隆慶六年某月某日，具官臣某伏蒙聖恩，以先臣禮部左侍郎兼翰林院學士薛瑄從祀孔廟，臣謹奉表稱謝者。伏以禮嚴祀事，殊恩下逮於先臣；道重儒林，曠典肇脩於盛世。議孚輿論，裁自宸衷；榮溢薦紳，感深末裔。臣某誠懽誠忭，稽首頓首。竊惟先聖教垂夫萬世，特廟酬功；羣賢品列於四科，分庭侑食。得其門者或寡，非其類則不
translation_en:
…seamless, and the diction is classical and elegant. This is someone skilled in crafting parallel couplets; I urgently recommend selecting him.]
Examiner and Instructor Wang's comment: [Memorials written in the examination hall are either superficial or prolix. This piece is well-grounded and finely polished, returning directly to great elegance; it follows the standards and models of the Song-dynasty masters.]
Examiner and Instructor Zhao's comment: [Classical and regular, worthy of recitation.]

On a certain day of a certain month in the sixth year of the Longqing reign (1572), Your servant So-and-so, holding full official title, having humbly received Your Sacred Grace ordering that our late ancestor, Left Vice Minister of Rites and concurrently Hanlin Academician Xue Xuan 薛瑄, be enshrined as an associate in the Temple of Confucius, respectfully presents this memorial to express gratitude.

Your servant humbly reflects that the rites are strict in matters of sacrifice, yet extraordinary grace has reached down to our late ancestor; the Way is revered among the forest of Confucians, and an unprecedented ceremony has been newly instituted in this flourishing age. The deliberations accorded with public opinion, and the decision came from the Imperial mind; the glory overflows among the gentry and officials, and gratitude runs deep in his distant descendants. Your servant So-and-so, truly joyful and truly elated, bows his head to the ground again and again.

Your servant humbly observes that the Former Sage handed down his teachings for ten thousand generations, and a special temple rewards his merit; the assembly of worthies was ranked according to the four categories of disciples, and they are arrayed in the courtyard to share in the sacrificial offerings. Those who find the gate to enter are perhaps few, and if one is not of that kind, the spirits will not…

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
歆錄韓愈於元豐望隆山斗益邵雍於景
定學究天人荀未臻堂室之區豈得陪廊
廡之末美新徵辛卽楊雄贊易在所當麾
獻賦乞憐縱劉向傳經亦終見黜蓋秩祀
昭隆師之
盛典而崇儒寓激世之微權〔臣〕祖瑄崛起河汾
遠宗濂洛脩身復性談道淑人著述無聞
未拓先民之緒躬行有得足開後覺之蒙
初奮迹於賢科繼守官於憲府持衡鄒魯
士還淳樸之風攬轡湖湘吏肅澄清之政
===
帝心於投杼旋申坐論之冤回
天意以賜環復拜
講筵之秩兼銜玉署叅
機密於中書晉貳春卿典
絲綸於秘閣逮正色無嫌於投鼠而高風遠
附於冥鴻環堵而居覺清脩之彌勵考槃
而樂守白賁以爲貞枕籍六經生平自適
punctuated: 歆。錄韓愈於元豐，望隆山斗；益邵雍於景定，學究天人。苟未臻堂室之區，豈得陪廊廡之末？美新徵辛，卽楊雄贊《易》，在所當麾；獻賦乞憐，縱劉向傳經，亦終見黜。蓋秩祀昭隆師之盛典，而崇儒寓激世之微權。〔臣〕祖瑄，崛起河汾，遠宗濂洛。脩身復性，談道淑人。著述無聞，未拓先民之緒；躬行有得，足開後覺之蒙。初奮迹於賢科，繼守官於憲府。持衡鄒魯，士還淳樸之風；攬轡湖湘，吏肅澄清之政。帝心於投杼，旋申坐論之冤；回天意以賜環，復拜講筵之秩。兼銜玉署，叅機密於中書；晉貳春卿，典絲綸於秘閣。逮正色無嫌於投鼠，而高風遠附於冥鴻。環堵而居，覺清脩之彌勵；考槃而樂，守白賁以爲貞。枕籍六經，生平自適；
translation_en:
… accept the sacrifice. Enrolling Han Yu 韓愈 in the Yuanfeng 元豐 era (1078–1085), his reputation was as lofty as Mount Tai and the Northern Dipper; adding Shao Yong 邵雍 in the Jingding 景定 era (1260–1264), his learning plumbed the realms of Heaven and humanity. If one has not reached the realm of the hall and inner chamber, how could one be permitted a place even at the end of the side galleries? Praising the Xin dynasty and inviting bitterness [?], even though Yang Xiong 楊雄 aided in the exposition of the Book of Changes (Yi 易), he ought to be waved away; presenting rhapsodies to beg for pity, even though Liu Xiang 劉向 transmitted the Classics, in the end he too was dismissed. For ordered sacrifices manifest the grand canon of honoring teachers, and exalting Confucian scholars embodies the subtle authority of rousing the world.

Your servant's grandfather Xuan (Xue Xuan 薛瑄) rose prominently from the Yellow and Fen Rivers (He-Fen 河汾) and took as his distant models the masters of the Lian and Luo Rivers (Lian-Luo 濂洛, i.e., Zhou Dunyi and the Cheng brothers). He cultivated his person and restored his innate nature, discoursing on the Way to improve others. Though little known for written compositions, having not expanded upon the threads of the ancients, he gained true attainment through personal practice, sufficient to enlighten the ignorance of later learners. At first he launched his career through the examination for the worthy, and subsequently held office in the Censorate. When he held the scales of evaluation as education intendant in Zou and Lu (Shandong), scholars returned to pure and simple customs; when he grasped the carriage reins on tour in Huxiang (Huguang), officials grew reverent under his governance of purification. Even if [something shook?] the Imperial mind like the mother dropping her shuttle, the injustice of his condemnation while discoursing on state affairs was soon redressed; turning back Heaven's intent by granting him thejade ring of recall, he was again appointed to the rank of the Classics Mat (Jiangyan 講筵). Concurrently holding a title in the Hanlin Academy, he participated in confidential affairs in the Grand Secretariat; promoted to Vice Minister of Rites, he took charge of drafting imperial utterances in the Secret Pavilion (Grand Secretariat). When with stern countenance he had no qualms about throwing stones at rats near prized vessels, his lofty spirit attached itself afar to the high-flying wild goose. Dwelling within four bare walls, he felt his pure cultivation become ever more strenuous; rejoicing in his secluded hut, he guarded unadorned simplicity as his constancy. Pillowed upon the Six Classics, throughout his life he found contentment in himself; …

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
險夷一節沒世名稱故當
肅皇嗣服之初已
採諸臣從祀之議
典維新以有待論旣久而自公玆蓋伏遇
皇帝陛下
日就月將
乾旋坤運
躬親耒耜先知稼穡之艱
臨幸辟廱獨謹庠序之敎旣
===
厲精於正學因
注意於脩文謂〔臣〕瑄爲二百年理學之宏儒
何止祀諸鄉校惟仲尼乃億萬載斯文之
盟主端宜附於宮牆爰渙
天章俾從廟食妥靈釋奠之側恍金聲玉振之
親承遊神宗廟之中儼江漢秋陽之載覩
兩楹共邃樂並聽於宮懸八簋攸陳禮同
中乎犧獻匪直褒崇旣往庶幾風勵將來
精爽如存幸吾道之未墜寵榮適至啟世
punctuated: 險夷一節，沒世名稱。故當肅皇嗣服之初，已採諸臣從祀之議。典維新以有待，論旣久而自公。玆蓋伏遇皇帝陛下，日就月將，乾旋坤運。躬親耒耜，先知稼穡之艱；臨幸辟廱，獨謹庠序之敎。旣厲精於正學，因注意於脩文。謂〔臣〕瑄爲二百年理學之宏儒，何止祀諸鄉校；惟仲尼乃億萬載斯文之盟主，端宜附於宮牆。爰渙天章，俾從廟食。妥靈釋奠之側，恍金聲玉振之親承；遊神宗廟之中，儼江漢秋陽之載覩。兩楹共邃，樂並聽於宮懸；八簋攸陳，禮同中乎犧獻。匪直褒崇旣往，庶幾風勵將來。精爽如存，幸吾道之未墜；寵榮適至，啟世…
translation_en:
…remained consistent in integrity through danger and ease alike, and his renown endures after his passing. Therefore, when the August Emperor Shizong (Suhuang 肅皇) first succeeded to the throne, he already adopted the officials' proposals to accord him auxiliary sacrifices in the Confucian Temple. Yet the newly instituted rite still awaited its moment, and as the discussion continued over a long period, public consensus naturally emerged.

Now, I humbly encounter Your Majesty the Emperor, advancing daily and monthly in achievement, revolving like Heaven and moving like Earth. Personally putting Your hand to the plowshare, You first understand the hardships of sowing and reaping; gracing the Imperial University (Piyong 辟廱) with Your presence, You take special care with the teachings of the schools. Having devoted Your energies to orthodox learning, You consequently turn Your attention to the cultivation of civil culture. Considering that Your servant's ancestor [Xue] Xuan 薛瑄 was a great Confucian scholar of the learning of principle (lixue 理學) over the past two hundred years, how could sacrifices to him be confined merely to the local schools? Since Confucius (Zhongni 仲尼) alone is the sovereign master of this culture of ours for hundreds of millions of years, it is truly fitting that he be attached within the walls of his temple.

Thereupon You issued a celestial proclamation, permitting him to share in the temple sacrifices. As his spirit rests beside the libation offerings (shidian 釋奠), it is as though he personally receives the music sounded by bronze bells and concluded by jade chimes; as his soul roams within the ancestral temple, it is as though he once again beholds the moral brilliance washed by the Yangzi and Han rivers and bleached by the autumn sun. Within the deep halls between the two pillars, he listens together to the music of the palace-suspended chimes; where the eight grain-vessels are arrayed, he shares alike in the rites of the sacrificial offerings. This not only honors and exalts the past, but may also inspire and encourage the future. His spirit and vitality seem present, rejoicing that our Way has not fallen to the ground; as this favor and glory arrive, they open up our family's generations-long…

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
德之彌昭臣屬在雲仍分叨章掖箕裘思
紹衣鉢無傳詒厥孫謀幸有讀書之録繩
其祖武慚無從政之才敢不益懋家聲期
以對揚
休命伏願
與人爲善
能自得師
進退古今挈諸儒之要領
兼總條貫集羣聖之大成
===
尊所聞行所知四海仰
純王之治
愼其終惟其始萬年享有道之長臣無任瞻
天仰
聖激切感戴之至謹奉
表稱
謝以
聞
第叅場
punctuated:
德之彌昭。臣屬在雲仍，分叨章掖，箕裘思紹，衣鉢無傳。詒厥孫謀，幸有《讀書》之録；繩其祖武，慚無從政之才。敢不益懋家聲，期以對揚休命！伏願與人爲善，能自得師。進退古今，挈諸儒之要領；兼總條貫，集羣聖之大成。尊所聞、行所知，四海仰純王之治；愼其終、惟其始，萬年享有道之長。臣無任瞻天仰聖、激切感戴之至，謹奉表稱謝以聞。

第叅場
translation_en:
…making the virtue of our family shine all the more brightly. Your servant belongs to the line of his distant descendants and by lot enjoys the privilege of a scholar's robes; though I wish to carry on the family trade, I have not inherited the mantle of his teachings. In the counsels he bequeathed to his descendants, we are fortunate to possess his Record of Reading Books (Dushu lu); yet in following in the footsteps of my ancestor, I am ashamed to lack the talent for governance. How dare I not strive all the more to uphold our family's reputation, hoping thereby to extol and answer Your beneficent mandate! I humbly pray that Your Majesty will join with others in doing good, and be able of Yourself to find true teachers; that You will weigh antiquity and the present, grasping the essential principles of all the Confucian scholars; and that You will comprehensively integrate their threads of meaning, synthesizing the great achievements of all the sages. May You honor what You have heard and practice what You know, so that all within the Four Seas look up to the rule of a pure king; may You be as careful of the end as You are mindful of the beginning, so that for ten thousand years the dynasty enjoys the enduring longevity of the Way. Your servant is overcome with the utmost emotion and gratitude as he gazes up at Heaven and reveres the Sage, and respectfully presents this memorial of thanks for the Emperor's hearing.

The Third Session

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
策五道
第一問
荆州俊
同考試官教諭李　批
〔我〕
皇上典學緝熙和敬並懋猶託物寓儆
望道未見之心也子能推廣其說以助
聖德之萬一忠藎之忱藹然溢乎詞矣敬錄以
獻
考試官教諭王　批
===
皇上稽古正學不忘
顧諟卽古先哲王何加焉篇內發揮詳盡而詞度馴雅取之
考試官教諭趙　批
〔問學深沉詞藻雅練藎風抱〕
獻納之具者
帝王之考鏡前烈也不貴有慕古之虛名
而貴有法古之實學夫含英漱潤娛情翰
墨陽浮慕之而飾太平之榮觀龍右文之
嘉問者所以爲名也篤仁義之塗遵三五
之軌精神孚貫若見羹牆而陟庭序者所
punctuated:
策五道
第一問
荆州俊
同考試官教諭李　批：〔我〕皇上典學緝熙，和敬並懋，猶託物寓儆，望道未見之心也。子能推廣其說，以助聖德之萬一，忠藎之忱，藹然溢乎詞矣。敬錄以獻。
考試官教諭王　批：皇上稽古正學，不忘顧諟，卽古先哲王何加焉？篇內發揮詳盡，而詞度馴雅，取之。
考試官教諭趙　批：〔問學深沉，詞藻雅練，藎夙抱〕獻納之具者。
帝王之考鏡前烈也，不貴有慕古之虛名，而貴有法古之實學。夫含英漱潤，娛情翰墨，陽浮慕之，而飾太平之榮觀，龍右文之嘉問者，所以爲名也；篤仁義之塗，遵三五之軌，精神孚貫，若見羹牆而陟庭序者，所
translation_en:
Five Policy Essays
First Question
Jing Zhoujun 荆州俊
Comment by Associate Examiner, Instructor Li: 〔Our〕 Sovereign pursues timeless learning with continuous radiance, cultivating both harmony and reverence, yet still uses physical objects to lodge admonitions—this is the mind of one who looks toward the Way as if he had not yet seen it. You are able to expand upon this idea to assist one ten-thousandth of His Sagely Virtue; your loyal and devoted sincerity gracefully overflows in your words. I respectfully record it for presentation to the throne.
Comment by Examiner, Instructor Wang: His Majesty examines antiquity to rectify learning, never forgetting to keep his gaze upon the clear mandate of Heaven—even the wise kings of ancient times, what could they add to this? Within the essay, the elaboration is thorough and exhaustive, and the diction and measure are refined and elegant. Selected.
Comment by Examiner, Instructor Zhao: 〔His learning and inquiry are deep and profound, his literary style is elegant and polished; truly one who has long cherished〕 the wherewithal to offer counsel to the throne.
When emperors and kings examine and mirror the illustrious achievements of their predecessors, what is valued is not holding an empty reputation for admiring antiquity, but possessing the substantive learning of modeling oneself upon antiquity. Savoring the blossoms and rinsing the mouth with the dew of literature, delighting one's feelings in brush and ink, outwardly and superficially admiring antiquity so as to adorn the glorious spectacle of an era of great peace and monopolize [?] the fine reputation of prizing civil culture—this is how one pursues reputation. Walking steadfastly upon the path of benevolence and righteousness, following the tracks of the Three Emperors and Five Sovereigns, with one's spirit sincerely penetrating their example as though seeing them in the soup and on the wall and ascending their courts and halls—this is how…

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
以爲實也學有名實斯德有純駁德有純
駁斯治有隆汙以實而不以名此古聖帝
明王所繇巍巍然煥然焉爽千載者也於乎
非
今日之盛其疇望哉嘗觀人主履至尊而制六
合一念不謹隱憂伏焉故其心無時而可
懈也奇衺靡麗快意當前者伺隙而狎進
故其學無地而可弛也古帝王知其然世
雖綦隆而不諱春冰秋駕之喻民雖熙皞
===
而不釋恫瘝勝予之懷德雖叡哲而不厭
逸欲傲虐之戒身雖隱獨而不忘臨汝時
保之訓於是君詢其臣臣迪其君而箴作
矣然箴何昉乎劉勰曰箴者所以攻疾防
患喻箴石也故傳說引瞑眩而虺言凡伯
即救藥而興喟古人取義蓋其淵矣粵稽
夏商二箴猶存與䇿是禹湯之憂勤殆不
止箕簴盤盂之儆已也辛甲虞箴體義更
備是成周之兢惕殆不止戶楹矛劍之規
punctuated: 以爲實也。學有名實，斯德有純駁；德有純駁，斯治有隆汙。以實而不以名，此古聖帝明王所繇巍巍然、煥然焉爽千載者也。於乎！非今日之盛，其疇望哉？嘗觀人主履至尊而制六合，一念不謹，隱憂伏焉，故其心無時而可懈也；奇衺靡麗、快意當前者，伺隙而狎進，故其學無地而可弛也。古帝王知其然，世雖綦隆，而不諱春冰秋駕之喻；民雖熙皞，而不釋恫瘝勝予之懷；德雖叡哲，而不厭逸欲傲虐之戒；身雖隱獨，而不忘臨汝時保之訓。於是君詢其臣，臣迪其君，而箴作矣。然箴何昉乎？劉勰曰：「箴者，所以攻疾防患，喻箴石也。」故傳說引瞑眩而虺言，凡伯即救藥而興喟，古人取義，蓋其淵矣。粵稽《夏》、《商》二箴猶存與䇿，是禹、湯之憂勤，殆不止箕簴盤盂之儆已也；辛甲《虞箴》體義更備，是成周之兢惕，殆不止戶楹矛劍之規…
translation_en:
…what constitutes the reality. When learning has name and reality, then virtue is either pure or mixed; when virtue is either pure or mixed, then governance is either flourishing or debased. Relying on reality rather than on name—this is whereby the sage emperors and enlightened kings of antiquity stood lofty and resplendent, illuminating [?] a thousand years. Alas! If not in the flourishing age of today, in whom else could we place our hopes?

I have observed that the ruler of men occupies the position of supreme veneration and controls the six directions; if a single thought is careless, hidden anxieties lie in ambush therein, and therefore his mind can at no time grow lax. Strange and perverse, extravagant and alluring things that gratify his desires before his eyes watch for an opening and press forward with familiarity, and therefore his learning has no place where it can be relaxed. The emperors and kings of antiquity knew this to be so. Thus, even when the age was at the height of prosperity, they did not shun the metaphors of treading on spring ice or driving an autumn chariot; even when the people were peaceful and contented, they did not let go of the concern over pain and distress or the fear of the common folk's surpassing [the ruler]; even when their virtue was perspicacious and wise, they did not tire of warnings against idleness, desire, arrogance, and cruelty; and even when they were alone in privacy, they did not forget the teachings that [God] looks down upon you and that one must constantly preserve [virtue]. Thereupon the sovereign inquired of his ministers, the ministers guided their sovereign, and admonitions (zhen 箴) were composed.

Yet how did admonitions originate? Liu Xie 劉勰 said: "Admonitions are that whereby one attacks ailments and guards against calamities, by analogy with acupuncture stones." Therefore Fu Yue 傅說 cited the dizziness caused by strong medicine in his earnest words [?], and the Earl of Fan 凡伯 sighed over administering medicine to save [the state]; the meaning taken by the ancients was profound indeed. When we examine how the two admonitions of Xia and Shang still survive in the bamboo slips [?], we see that the anxious diligence of Yu 禹 and Tang 湯 scarcely stopped merely at the warnings inscribed on bell-frames, basins, and bowls. In Xin Jia's 辛甲 "Admonition of the Huntsman" (Yu zhen 虞箴), the form and meaning were even more complete; thus the cautious vigilance of the Zhou dynasty scarcely stopped merely at the injunctions inscribed on doors, pillars, spears, and swords…

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
已也風敎房皇奕世載德卽篳路藍縷之
楚桑間濮上之衛亦能作在勤之箴以訓
民納箴御之箴而悔過庶幾哉先王之遺
意焉叔季以旋蓋亦各有作矣顧或組繪
雖工而格心之道未豫或告語徒切而遇
巻之情則疎太宗覽張蘊古大寶箴而旌
其直翠微遼左之役則靡究於躬行也敬
宗讀李德裕丹扆箴而褒其忠驪山魚藻
之遊則恱巽言而不繹矣裴諝睹德宗刑
===
罰失中而獻獄官箴辭亦美矣然猜忌成
性君子譏之趙師民因仁宗用兵西夏而
獻勸講箴意非不勤矣然優柔不振君子
有遺論焉方其借事陳規感時寓諷豈不
自謂憂危之遐矩交儆之微音哉乃美疢
易深惡石難入藉令矇瞽不停吟師工不
輟誦祇爲觀聽之具爾矣欲回皇心於粹
白翼治績於昭登其可得哉我
天子英資首出統一聖眞
punctuated: 已也。風敎房皇，奕世載德，卽篳路藍縷之楚、桑間濮上之衛，亦能作《在勤之箴》以訓民，納箴御之箴而悔過，庶幾哉先王之遺意焉！叔季以旋，蓋亦各有作矣。顧或組繪雖工，而格心之道未豫；或告語徒切，而遇巻之情則疎。太宗覽張蘊古《大寶箴》而旌其直，翠微、遼左之役，則靡究於躬行也；敬宗讀李德裕《丹扆箴》而褒其忠，驪山、魚藻之遊，則恱巽言而不繹矣。裴諝睹德宗刑罰失中，而獻《獄官箴》，辭亦美矣；然猜忌成性，君子譏之。趙師民因仁宗用兵西夏，而獻《勸講箴》，意非不勤矣；然優柔不振，君子有遺論焉。方其借事陳規，感時寓諷，豈不自謂憂危之遐矩、交儆之微音哉？乃美疢易深，惡石難入，藉令矇瞽不停吟，師工不輟誦，祇爲觀聽之具爾矣。欲回皇心於粹白，翼治績於昭登，其可得哉？我天子英資首出，統一聖眞，
translation_en: … only that. Moral instruction spread grandly, and generation after generation upheld virtue; even Chu, which began in brushwood carts and tattered clothes, and Wei, notorious for the airs of Sangjian and the Pu River, were able to compose the "Admonition on Diligence" (Zaiqin zhi zhen) to instruct the people, and to accept the admonition of the charioteer and repent of faults—how close this was to the legacy of the former kings! From the eras of decline onward, each age likewise had its own compositions. Yet in some cases, although the ornate diction was skillful, the way of rectifying the sovereign's heart was not prepared in advance; in others, the counsel was earnest in vain, while the sentiment of receptive engagement [?] remained distant. Emperor Taizong of Tang perused Zhang Yungu's "Admonition on the Great Treasure" (Dabao zhen) and commended his forthrightness, yet in building the Cuiwei Palace and campaigning in Liaodong, he failed to carry those principles through in personal practice. Emperor Jingzong of Tang read Li Deyu's "Admonitions of the Cinnabar Screen" (Danyi zhen) and praised his loyalty, yet in his excursions to Mount Li and the Yuzao Palace, he was pleased by compliant words without reforming himself. Pei Xu witnessed Emperor Dezong's punishments losing their proper balance and presented the "Admonition for Judicial Officials" (Yuguan zhen); its wording was indeed fine, yet because suspicion and jealousy had become the emperor's nature, noble men criticized it. Zhao Shimin, on account of Emperor Renzong of Song employing troops against Western Xia, presented the "Admonition on Encouraging Classical Lectures" (Quanjiang zhen); his intention was by no means lacking in earnestness, yet because the emperor remained indecisive and unenergetic, noble men still had lingering criticisms. When those authors borrowed events to set forth rules and responded to the times to lodge remonstrances, did they not consider their works to be far-reaching standards of anxious concern and subtle notes of mutual admonition? Yet pleasant ailments easily deepen, and bitter stone needles are hard to take; even if the blind musicians never ceased chanting and the music masters never stopped reciting, such words would merely serve as ornaments for sight and hearing. If one wished thereby to restore the imperial mind to pure whiteness and assist administrative achievements to rise in glorious brilliance, how could that be attained? Our Son of Heaven stands preeminent with heroic endowments, unifying sage perfection; …

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
宵衣求理至勤也
萬幾躬決至斷也閶澤汪濊至仁也
書大經大法與十二事至戒也褒表循吏列
百官於屏至明也
皇稜震疊九夷解辮至武也試以古事揆之
今土木罷營鼛鼓弗作
離宮別館虛而不御寧有如大寶箴所謂瑤
臺瓊室者乎減服官卻貢獻近郊無誇胡
羽獵之行
===
內庭絕魚龍角抵之戲寧有如冊扆箴所謂
宴遊侈汰者乎
欽恤之令歲下道靡赭衣吏鮮橋虔寧有如獄
官箴所謂深文巧傳者乎造膝沃心歡同
魚水金華虎觀罔間寒燠寧有如勸講箴
所謂不酌古道者乎卽使蘊古操觚德裕
握牘裴諝師民之徒日簪筆持槖於側且
將易箴爲頌以昭示乎無極況能飛輕塵
於喬嶽挹勺潤於滄溟哉我
punctuated: 宵衣求理，至勤也；萬幾躬決，至斷也；閶澤汪濊，至仁也；書大經大法與十二事，至戒也；褒表循吏，列百官於屏，至明也；皇稜震疊，九夷解辮，至武也。試以古事揆之：今土木罷營，鼛鼓弗作，離宮別館，虛而不御，寧有如《大寶箴》所謂「瑤臺瓊室」者乎？減服官，卻貢獻，近郊無誇胡羽獵之行，內庭絕魚龍角抵之戲，寧有如《冊扆箴》所謂「宴遊侈汰」者乎？欽恤之令歲下，道靡赭衣，吏鮮橋虔，寧有如《獄官箴》所謂「深文巧傳」者乎？造膝沃心，歡同魚水，金華虎觀，罔間寒燠，寧有如《勸講箴》所謂「不酌古道」者乎？卽使蘊古操觚，德裕握牘，裴諝、師民之徒，日簪筆持槖於側，且將易箴爲頌，以昭示乎無極，況能飛輕塵於喬嶽、挹勺潤於滄溟哉！我
translation_en: …dressing before dawn to seek good governance, he is supremely diligent; personally deciding a myriad affairs of state, he is supremely resolute; his imperial favor flowing vast and deep, he is supremely benevolent; writing out the great standards and great laws along with the Twelve Matters, he is supremely vigilant; commending and honoring upright officials and listing the hundred officials on a screen, he is supremely discerning; his imperial majesty striking awe afar so that the Nine Yi tribes unbraid their hair in submission, he is supremely martial. Let us measure the present against those ancient matters: today, construction projects have been halted, the great construction drums do not sound, and detached palaces and secondary lodges stand empty and unused—how could there be anything like what the Admonition on the Great Treasure (Dabao zhen) calls "terraces of jasper and chambers of jade"? Having reduced the agencies for imperial garments and rejected tribute offerings, the near suburbs see no plumed hunts staged to boast before the northern tribes, and the inner court has put an end to theatrical spectacles of fish-dragons and wrestling—how could there be anything like what the Admonition for the Throne Screen (Ceyi zhen) calls "extravagance and excess in banqueting and pleasure-trips"? With edicts of reverent compassion issued year after year, the roads are free of convicts in ochre-dyed clothes and officials rarely engage in perverse extortion [? 橋虔 for 矯虔]—how could there be anything like what the Admonition for Prison Officials (Yuguan zhen) calls "harsh application of the letter of the law and artful fabrication of charges" [? 巧傳 for 巧傅]? Drawing close to his ministers for heart-enriching counsel, sharing a joy like that of fish and water, in the Jinhua Hall and White Tiger Pavilion without interruption through winter's cold or summer's heat—how could there be anything like what the Admonition Encouraging Imperial Lectures (Quanjiang zhen) calls "failing to draw upon the ways of antiquity"? Even if Zhang Yungu were to take up his writing tablet, Li Deyu to grasp his boards, and men such as Pei Xu and Zhao Shimin were daily to wear brushes in their caps and hold document sacks by his side, they would instead change their admonitions into eulogies to proclaim his glory unto eternity—how much less could they add a speck of flying dust to a lofty mountain or pour a spoonful of moisture into the vast ocean! Our…

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
天子聖不自聖兢業愈嚴謂
深宮燕閒不可有慢遊也時
御便殿而恭默以凝神謂細旃廣廈不可有閒
隙也日
繙經史而多識以蓄德謂覽今不若監古之
爲優也溥稽周詩取
雝肅之旨而肇
錫以嘉名謂稱名不若思義之爲切也
特命輔臣撰書屛之箴而
===
顧諟以自儆弗師保而嚴弗旅賁而諫日月
就將緝奝緝熙持此絜德羲軒錄功姚姒
無難也愚恐生伏處奧漢末由窺
天府秘館之藏竊計崇論閎議法語讜言凡可
以副
明主之虛懷攄蓋臣之極悃者箴之說具備矣
圭箄何知而敢贅一辭乎竊嘗聞之乃言
厎績而夏長楙儀式文典而周道穠人君
所貴於法古者非欲法其名也欲法其所
punctuated:
天子聖不自聖，兢業愈嚴：謂深宮燕閒，不可有慢遊也，時御便殿，而恭默以凝神；謂細旃廣廈，不可有閒隙也，日繙經史，而多識以蓄德；謂覽今不若監古之爲優也，溥稽《周詩》，取雝肅之旨，而肇錫以嘉名；謂稱名不若思義之爲切也，特命輔臣撰書屛之箴，而顧諟以自儆。弗師保而嚴，弗旅賁而諫，日月就將，緝奝緝熙，持此絜德羲軒、錄功姚姒，無難也。

愚恐生伏處奧漢，末由窺天府秘館之藏，竊計崇論閎議、法語讜言，凡可以副明主之虛懷、攄蓋臣之極悃者，箴之說具備矣，圭箄何知，而敢贅一辭乎？竊嘗聞之：乃言厎績而夏長楙，儀式文典而周道穠。人君所貴於法古者，非欲法其名也，欲法其所
translation_en:
… the Son of Heaven, though a sage, does not regard himself as a sage, growing ever stricter in cautious diligence. Holding that in the leisure of the deep palace there must be no negligent roaming, he regularly visits the side halls, reverent and silent so as to concentrate his spirit. Holding that upon the fine felt rugs of the spacious halls there must be no idle intervals, he daily unrolls the Classics and Histories, learning widely so as to accumulate virtue. Holding that surveying the present is not as advantageous as mirroring the past, he broadly examined the Zhou Odes (Zhou shi), took the meaning of "harmonious and reverent" (yong su), and initiated the bestowal of auspicious names. Holding that bearing a name is not as pertinent as pondering its meaning, he specially commanded the Grand Secretaries to compose admonitions to be inscribed on screens, keeping his gaze upon them for self-warning. Strict without needing a Tutor or Guardian, remonstrated with without needing the Brave-as-Tigers Guards, advancing day and month in continuous and luminous devotion—holding fast to this, it is no difficult thing to match the virtue of Fuxi and Xuanyuan or record achievements alongside Yao and Yu.

Yet this foolish scholar [?], dwelling humbly in rustic obscurity, has no way to peer into the collections of the imperial treasury and secret archives. I privately reckon that lofty discourses and grand deliberations, model words and forthright counsels—all that can answer the enlightened ruler's receptive mind and express a loyal minister's utmost sincerity—are already fully provided in the explanations of those admonitions. What does a man behind a wicker gate know, that he would dare add a superfluous word? Yet I have heard it said: when words can be brought to successful performance, the growth of Xia flourishes; when one takes the statutes of King Wen as a model and norm, the Way of Zhou abounds. What a ruler values in modeling himself on antiquity is not the desire to imitate its names, but the desire to imitate that whereby…

title: 萬曆七年山西鄉試錄
text:
以爲名也人臣稽古以匡君者非欲法其
迹也欲因迹而得其意也方今
孝養
慈闈化行
宮壼國儼乎三朝刑于之風而極其雝矣然
易之家人曰閑有家悔亡則在宮若不專
於尚和也
躬親
廟饗薦瓚受釐固宛乎惠于宗公之度而極其
===
肅矣然詩之下武曰世德作求永言孝思
則在廟若不貴於徒敬也愚以爲關雎之
情非不爭尤宜重雞鳴簪珥之益常棣之
誼非不洽尤宜鑒削桐共輦之嬉御下未
甞少恩然嚬笑必謹而譽嘉樹假臂鷹以
市寵者勿得施睦親未甞不厚然威柄無
移而請考工奪沁園以恣睢者勿得肆如
此則愛隆非過昵恩溥非過私而和其不
流矣乎瞻
punctuated: 以爲名也。人臣稽古以匡君者，非欲法其迹也，欲因迹而得其意也。方今孝養慈闈，化行宮壼，國儼乎三朝刑于之風，而極其雝矣。然《易》之〈家人〉曰：「閑有家，悔亡。」則在宮若不專於尚和也。躬親廟饗，薦瓚受釐，固宛乎惠于宗公之度，而極其肅矣。然《詩》之〈下武〉曰：「世德作求，永言孝思。」則在廟若不貴於徒敬也。愚以爲〈關雎〉之情非不爭，尤宜重〈雞鳴〉簪珥之益；〈常棣〉之誼非不洽，尤宜鑒削桐共輦之嬉。御下未甞少恩，然嚬笑必謹，而譽嘉樹、假臂鷹以市寵者，勿得施；睦親未甞不厚，然威柄無移，而請考工、奪沁園以恣睢者，勿得肆。如此則愛隆非過昵，恩溥非過私，而和其不流矣乎！瞻
translation_en:
… whereby they earned their reputation. When ministers examine antiquity to rectify their ruler, it is not that they wish him to imitate its outward traces, but that they wish him to grasp the underlying intent through those traces.

At present, the Emperor filially tends to the Empress Dowager's quarters and causes his transforming influence to prevail throughout the palace women's apartments; indeed, [read 固 for 國?] this manifests with dignity the ancient custom of inquiring thrice daily after one's parents' health and setting an example for one's consort, reaching the very height of harmony. Yet the "Family" (Jiaren) hexagram of the Book of Changes (Yi) says: "With regulation in the family, remorse disappears." Thus, within the palace, it seems one should not exclusively prize harmony alone.

He personally attends the ancestral temple sacrifices, offering the jade libation ladle and receiving the ceremonial blessings; truly, this reproduces the bearing of conforming to the ancestral dukes, reaching the very height of solemnity. Yet the ode "Successors to Martial Merit" (Xiawu) in the Book of Odes (Shi) says: "For generations they have striven to match their forebears' virtue, forever cherishing filial thoughts." Thus, within the ancestral temple, it seems one does not value mere outward reverence alone.
